translation_en:
Sheng Bin, registered with Dahe Guard in the directly administered region, belonged to a military household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Anzhi. Second in birth order, he was aged twenty-nine and was born on the nineteenth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Cunren, his grandfather Shixian, and his father Zhongjie; his father's former wives were née Pan and née Hu, and his mother was née Wang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Guang and his younger brother Sen. He married a woman née Wang and subsequently a woman née Shen. He ranked thirtieth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and ninety-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhou Bian, from Gaomi County, Jiaozhou Subprefecture, Laizhou Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a military household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Shizhi. First in birth order, he was aged thirty-nine and was born on the second day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Jide, his grandfather Cheng, his father Zheng, and his mother née Wang. His father was living and his mother deceased. His younger brother was Song. He married a woman née Ru. He ranked twenty-seventh in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 344th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Du Zhong, from Heyin County, Zhengzhou Subprefecture, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, belonged to a military household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Shichen. Third in birth order, he was aged thirty-eight and was born on the twenty-second day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Caixing, his grandfather Gong, an Instructor in the Yin-yang School, his father Zhen, and his mother née Wang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Rang and Xin. He married a woman née Zhang. He ranked fortieth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 136th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shi Xiao, from □□ County, Huai'an Prefecture, in □□ [place names illegible], belonged to a military household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Rites; his courtesy name was Tingzhong. First in birth order, he was aged twenty-seven and was born on the seventh day of the intercalary ninth month. His great-grandfather was Guping; his grandfather Jingyu was posthumously appointed Left Assistant Administration Commissioner; his father Min was Right Vice Administration Commissioner in a Provincial Administration Commission; and his mother, née Pan, was granted the title Lady of Respect. Both parents and at least one grandparent were living. His elder brother Jin was an Instructor. He married a woman née Guo. He ranked eightieth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 205th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Yuan Tan 袁潭, of Tiantai County, Taizhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a household of illegible registration category (□□). An Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he had the courtesy name Junzhi and ranked third in his family; his age is unclear in the transcription (□□十) [?], and he was born on the twentieth day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Xuanzhong, his grandfather Wenmei, his father Yingshan, and his mother Lady Chen. His father was living and his mother deceased. His elder brothers were You and Ding, and his younger brother was 𤇍 [reading uncertain]. He married Lady Ma. He placed seventy-first in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 261st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Xun 劉遜, of Anfu County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a Confucian scholar household. An added-quota student of the county school specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he had the courtesy name Shirang, ranked fifth in his family, and was twenty-seven years old, born on an illegible day (□□) of the intercalary ninth month. His great-grandfather was Zimao, his grandfather Suxuan (granted the title of Supervising Secretary), his father Lunhui, and his mother Lady Wang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Xuan, Yu, Jin, and Er; his younger brothers were Po and Xia. He married Lady Zhu. He placed seventeenth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 183rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ye Ying 葉應, of Guishan County, Huizhou Prefecture, Guangdong, belonged to a civilian household. A county school student specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he had the courtesy name Ziwei, ranked second in his family, and was forty-six years old, born on the first day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Mao (an Assistant Prefect), his grandfather Guangzu, his father De, and his mother Lady Liu. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Zhong, and his younger brothers were Shu and Que. He married Lady Xue. He placed forty-ninth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 309th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shi Shu 施恕, of Kaihua County, Quzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to an artisan household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Changes, he had the courtesy name Mianren, ranked fourteenth in his family, and was forty-one years old, born on the ninth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Junsui, his grandfather Wenzhen, his father Jingrong, his mother Lady Hu, and his stepmother Lady Xiang. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Maocong. He married Lady Yu. He placed seventy-third in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 330th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Xia Zuo, courtesy name Tianxi, was a National University student registered in a civilian household in Dangtu County, Taiping Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region; he specialized in the Classic of Poetry, ranked second among his brothers, and was aged forty-three, born on the eighth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Tongliu, his grandfather Zheng, his father Benyuan, and his mother née Zhu; both parents were living, his elder brother was Chun and his younger brother Lu, his wife was née Tao, and he placed eighty-second in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 282nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Wei, courtesy name Tingxiu, was a National University student registered in a military household in Yishui County, Ju Subprefecture, Qingzhou Prefecture, Shandong; he specialized in the Classic of Documents, ranked fifth among his brothers, and was aged twenty-nine, born on an illegible day (□) of the intercalary first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wentong, his grandfather Shicheng, his father Rong, and his mother née Gao; both parents were deceased, his elder brothers were Hui (an Honorary Official for Philanthropy), Zheng, Chong, and Heng (a Battalion Commander), his wife was née Wu, and he placed sixteenth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 179th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ma Long, courtesy name Wenxiang, was a National University student registered in a military household in Qidong County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong; he specialized in the Classic of Documents, ranked third among his brothers, and was aged twenty-nine, born on the twenty-seventh day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Dexin, his grandfather Xuan, his father Kui (a Subprefectural Judge), and his mother née Wang; both parents were living, his elder brothers were Pi and Qing, his wife was née Xin, and he placed forty-third in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 107th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhai Neng, courtesy name Benshan, was a National University student registered in a civilian household in Hejian County, Hejian Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region; he specialized in the Classic of Poetry, ranked first among his brothers, and was aged forty-three, born on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Cheng, his grandfather Yong, his father Xin, and his mother née Zhao; his father was deceased and his mother living, his younger brothers were Gan, Qing, Lian, Jun, and Xiu, he married a woman née Jia and subsequently a woman née Niu, and he placed at an illegible rank (□□) in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 117th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
□ Zeng (surname illegible), courtesy name Yizhong, was registered in □□ County (name illegible), Baoding Prefecture, in the Metropolitan Region, in an official household. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged twenty-six, and born on the twenty-fourth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was De, a Company Commander; his grandfather was Youxia; his father was Liang; and his mother was née Ma. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Tang and Cheng, and his wife was née Tang. He placed seventy-ninth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 291st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Bai Jin, courtesy name Yingzhi, was registered in Shanyin County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Documents, he was fourth in birth order, aged thirty, and born on the sixteenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Guoguang, a Department Magistrate; his grandfather was Yanming; and his father was Leize. His father's former wife was née Yu, and his mother was née Niu. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Lian, Min, and Yu, and his wife was née Ge. He placed fiftieth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 162nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Jianzhi, courtesy name Mingzhong, was registered in Shanyin County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he was second in birth order, aged thirty-nine, and born on the eleventh day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shou; his grandfather was Junyao; his father was Shen; and his mother was née Cheng. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Kuangzhi, and his wife was née Hu. He placed sixteenth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 200th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Cunli, courtesy name Yonghe, was registered with the Jiezhou Battalion of the Qinzhou Guard, Shaanxi, in a military household. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Documents, he was third in birth order, aged twenty-eight, and born on the twenty-first day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhen; his grandfather was Rong; his father was Yu, an Instructor; and his mother was née Xie. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brother was Cunren, his younger brother was Cunyi, and his wife was née Zhang. He placed second in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 212th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Liu Jun 劉濬, courtesy name Xiyuan, was from □□ County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi, registered in an official household, and a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals; he ranked tenth among his brothers, was aged forty-two, and was born on the sixteenth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Lanfang, his grandfather Mengxun, and his father Zigui; his father's principal wife was née Yin and his birth mother née Liu; his father was deceased and his mother living; his elder brothers were Lüe, Chong, and Zhao, his younger brother was Yong, and his wife was née Xu; he placed sixteenth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and eightieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Su Zhong 蘇鐘, courtesy name Zhongzai, was from Longyan County, Zhangzhou Prefecture, Fujian, registered in a civilian household, and held a status recorded as 國□□, probably student of the Directorate of Education [?], specializing in the Book of Odes; he ranked second among his brothers, was aged forty, and was born on the twenty-eighth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zongming, Associate Salt Distribution Commissioner, his grandfather Kongcheng, and his father Yuan; his father's former wife was née Chen and his mother née Yang; both parents were living; his elder brother was Jun, and he married a woman née Deng and subsequently a woman née Chen; he placed twenty-fourth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 233rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Wen 吳文, courtesy name Zaidao, was from Luling County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi, registered in a civilian household, and a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes; he ranked fourth among his brothers, was aged forty-one, and was born on the twenty-third day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yihe, his grandfather Ruli, and his father Boxun; his father's former wife was née Shen and his mother née Xiao; both parents were deceased; his elder brothers were Pu, a student of the Directorate of Education, Jie, and Huan, and his wife was née Liu; he placed nineteenth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination, and his Metropolitan Examination rank is recorded incompletely as 一百三十□ (130–139 [?]).

Zhou Xu 周敘, courtesy name Tianxu, was from Nanhai County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, registered in a civilian household, and a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes; he ranked third among his brothers, was aged thirty-four, and was born on the sixteenth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhaoyue, his grandfather Yanbin, and his father Shun; his mother was née Xie; both parents were living; his elder brothers were Jing and Fu, and his wife was née Xu; he placed seventh in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 329th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zheng Lun, courtesy name Tingzhang, was registered in a military household in Yuzhou, Datong Prefecture, Shanxi, and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. First in birth order, he was aged thirty-six and was born on the twenty-second day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ming, his grandfather Jie, and his father Feng, an honorary official; his mother was née Liu. His father was deceased and his mother living. His younger brothers were Shen and Ji, the latter an Astrological Technician. He married a woman née Yang. He placed fifth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and fifty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Jiang Qin, courtesy name Shiqin, was registered in a military household in Shangrao County, Guangxin Prefecture, Jiangxi, and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents. Fifth in birth order, he was aged forty-one and was born on the twenty-eighth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Dejing, his grandfather Jianshan, and his father Shangguan; his father's principal wife was née Fu, and his birth mother was née Wang. His parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Ying, Xian, Zhong, and Qi. He married a woman née Xu and subsequently married another woman née Xu. He placed fourth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 265th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Jing, courtesy name Tianchang, was registered in a military household of the Tengxiang Right Guard and was a native of Chang'an County, Shaanxi. He was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. First in birth order, he was aged twenty-seven and was born on the twenty-third day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhong, his grandfather Yu, and his father Shan, an honorary official; his mother was née Wang. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Lun, Jin, Shen, Shou, Yan, and Chuo. He married a woman née Li. He placed thirty-third in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and twenty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Hui, courtesy name Fengju, was registered in a military household of the Yunnan Central Guard in Yunnan and was a native of Kunshan County in the directly administered metropolitan region. He was a student of the Yunnan Prefectural School specializing in the Book of Changes. Fourth in birth order, he was aged twenty-three and was born on the sixth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yangang, his grandfather Deyi, and his father Ji; his mother was née Zheng. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Yu, Yi, and Ao. He was betrothed to a woman née Wang. He placed twenty-seventh in the Yunnan Provincial Examination and 348th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Pu 陳溥 was registered in □□ County, Runing Prefecture, Henan, in a military household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he had the courtesy name □bo, was first in birth order, and was thirty-five years old, born on the twenty-eighth [?] day of the third month (transcribed as 二八). His great-grandfather was Zhongkuan; his grandfather, Jingxian; and his father, Lian, a department magistrate. His father's former wife was née Han, his mother née Zhang, and his stepmother née Yan. Both parents were deceased. His younger brother was Yuan, and he married a woman née Yuan 元. He placed fifty-seventh in the Henan Provincial Examination and 122nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xie Gui 謝珪 was registered in Haiyang County, Chaozhou Prefecture, Guangdong, in a military household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Changes, he had the courtesy name Yunzhi, was third in birth order, and was forty-two years old, born on the fourth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Weixian; his grandfather, Wenyuan; and his father, Nongji. His father's former wife was née Chen, and his mother was née Su. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Zongyu, an instructor, and Xiong. He married a woman née Xing. He placed eighteenth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and ninety-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ma Xiu 馬琇 was registered in Luoshan County, Xinyang Department, Runing Prefecture, Henan, in an artisan household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he had the courtesy name Tianxu, was fourth in birth order, and was thirty-six years old, born on the sixth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Yun; his grandfather, Dehe; and his father, Rong. His mother was née He, and his stepmother was née Lu. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Tengxiao, Jun, and Li, and his younger brother was Lin. He married a woman née Qu and was subsequently betrothed to □□. He placed third in the Henan Provincial Examination; his Metropolitan Examination rank is recorded as 一百二十□□, apparently 120-something [?].

Ma Mao 馬懋 was registered in the Tengxiang Right Guard in an official household and was a native of Guantao County, Shandong. An additional student of the Shuntian Prefectural School specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he had the courtesy name Zhaode, was first in birth order, and was twenty-one years old, born on the twenty-first day of the first month. His great-grandfather Yu and grandfather Jun were each posthumously granted the title of vice commander-in-chief. His father, whose name is illegible, held the honorary designation of Righteous Official; his mother was née Pan. Both parents were living. His younger brothers are recorded as De and □□ [?]. He married a woman née Zhai. His rank in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination is partly illegible, recorded as □□十八名; he placed fifty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

He was first in birth order, aged forty-one, and born on the tenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wenzhi, his grandfather Rui, and his father Zhicong; his mother was née Wang. His mother was still living, and his father was deceased. He married a woman née Liu and subsequently a woman née Yan. He placed fifty-fifth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and fourteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Li, courtesy name Jingxian, was registered in Yuhang County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Rites. He was third in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the sixth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhou, his grandfather Zeshan, and his father Xing; his mother was née Li, and his stepmother’s surname is illegible. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Ren and Yi. He married a woman née Ye. He placed twenty-seventh in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 343rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xiong Jing, courtesy name Zaidao, was registered in Macheng County, Huangzhou Prefecture, Huguang, in a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals. He was first in birth order, aged thirty-eight, and born on the twenty-second day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yongchang, his grandfather Quan, and his father Zimin; his mother was née Duan. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Lun, Hong, and Shou. He married a woman née Zhu (主) [?] and subsequently a woman née Chen. He placed ninth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 258th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shi Ying, courtesy name Tingzhen, was registered in Jishan County, Jiangzhou Subprefecture, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, in a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Classic of Poetry. He was first in birth order, aged thirty, and born on the nineteenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhongli, his grandfather Boshan, and his father Gui; his mother was née Yang. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Qi and Huan. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed sixty-second in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 259th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Yin Ling 尹陵, courtesy name Rufu, was from Jingshan County, Anlu Subprefecture, Huguang, and registered in a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he was sixth in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the sixth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wuben; his grandfather, Chuandao; and his father, Zhe, an Instructor. His father's principal wife was Lady Liu, and his birth mother was Lady Shi. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Gu, a Magistrate, Guan, Yuan, Biao, and Duan; his younger brother was Han. He married Lady Liu. He ranked fifty-fifth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and forty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Cheng 張宬, courtesy name Zonghui, was from Zhangqiu County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, and registered in a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he was second in birth order, aged twenty-six, and born on the twenty-first day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shilin, an Administrative Assistant in a Salt Distribution Commission; his grandfather, Lu; and his father, Yun, an honorary official recognized for charitable contributions. His father's principal wife was Lady Feng, and his birth mother's surname is illegible (□). His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brother was Fou (哹) [?]. He married Lady Gu. He ranked forty-fourth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 148th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Bao Nai 包鼐, courtesy name Ruhe, was from Jiaxing County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, and registered in a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Documents, he was second in birth order, aged thirty-one, and born on the twenty-eighth day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Chengfu; his grandfather, Gui, who had been granted the privilege of wearing official cap and girdle under provisions for imperial favor; and his father, Jun. His mother was Lady Wang, and his stepmother's surname is illegible (□). Both parents were living. His elder brother Ding was a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the same examination year; his younger brothers were Zi and Mi. He married Lady Gu. He ranked eighty-fourth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and one hundredth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Huang Yi 黃頤, courtesy name Yangde, was from Puqi County, Wuchang Prefecture, Huguang, and registered in a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he was fourth in birth order, aged forty-five, and born on the twentieth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yi; his grandfather, Yue; and his father's name is illegible (□). His mother was Lady Su. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Yu and Qian; the names of his younger brother or brothers are illegible (□□□□). He married Lady Xu. His rank in the Huguang Provincial Examination is partially illegible (□十一, ending in eleven); he ranked 207th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Rui, courtesy name Shixiang, was from Ji [county?], Weihui Prefecture, Henan; two illegible characters obscure the county designation and registration category [?]. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged forty-one, and born on the second day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Huan, his grandfather Ying, his father Feng, and his mother née Guo; his father was deceased and his mother living. His younger brothers were Xiang, Xiu, and Zan. He married a woman née Zhao and subsequently a woman née Zhou. He ranked fifty-first in the Henan Provincial Examination and 302nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zheng Kui, courtesy name Defu, was from She County, Huizhou Prefecture, in the directly administered region, with civilian registration. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he was third in birth order, aged thirty-nine, and born on the sixteenth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Yang, his grandfather Daotong, his father Fuling, and his mother née Wang; both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Jun and his younger brother Yan. He married a woman née Fang and subsequently a woman née Hu. He ranked fourth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 292nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Huang Su, courtesy name Jingfu, was from Liuhe County, Yingtian Prefecture, with civilian registration. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Rites, he was fifth in birth order, aged thirty-seven, and born on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Dehui, his grandfather Tong, his father Qiong, his mother née Ye, and his stepmother a woman whose surname is illegible; both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were De, Dan, and Can. He married a woman née Zhao. He ranked twenty-second in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 216th in the Metropolitan Examination [the character following the number is illegible].

Du Zheng, courtesy name Siqi, was from Pingyang County, Wenzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, with civilian registration. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-six, and born on the thirteenth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Mengchu, his grandfather Liya, his father Chen, his mother née Mao, and his stepmother née Shen; his father was deceased and his mother living. His younger brothers are transcribed as Pie, Jie, Juan, Gong, Zhen, Dan, and Qin [?]. He married a woman née Liu and subsequently a woman née Chen. He ranked seventy-seventh in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 171st in the Metropolitan Examination.

譚肅〔貫山東兖州府東平州壽張縣，民籍，國子生，治書經，字本恭，行三，年四十一，八月十九日生〕。曾祖成，祖有道，父智，母周氏。永感下，兄整、敞，娶王氏。山東鄉試第二十九名，會試第六十一名。

盛慶〔貫河南汝寧府西平縣，匠籍，國子生，治詩經，字仲禧，行二，年四十四，十二月二十九日生〕。曾祖成甫，祖景芳，父敏〔推官〕，母王氏。具慶下，兄哲，弟元，繼娶涂氏。河南鄉試第五十一名，會試第七十九名。

劉清〔貫江西九江府德化縣，軍籍，國子生，治詩經，字一之，行三，年四十，十一月初十日生〕。曾祖壽一，祖英，父貴，母蕭氏。具慶下，兄洪、澄，弟明、齊，娶周氏。江西鄉試第七十八名，會試第一百七十三名。
translation_en:
Bian Hui 卞譓, courtesy name Weixin, was from Wujin County, Changzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, registered in a civilian household; he was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Rites, aged thirty-six, and born on the first day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Boxiang, his grandfather Deyuan, his father Shuxian, and his mother née Zhuang; both parents were deceased; his elder brother was Hong, and his wife was née Cheng; he ranked 108th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 303rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tan Su 譚肅, courtesy name Bengong, was from Shouzhang County, Dongping Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, registered in a civilian household; he was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, third in birth order, aged forty-one, and born on the nineteenth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Cheng, his grandfather Youdao, his father Zhi, and his mother née Zhou; both parents were deceased; his elder brothers were Zheng and Chang, and his wife was née Wang; he ranked 29th in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 61st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Sheng Qing 盛慶, courtesy name Zhongxi, was from Xiping County, Runing Prefecture, Henan, registered in an artisan household; he was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, second in birth order, aged forty-four, and born on the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Chengfu, his grandfather Jingfang, his father Min〔Prefectural Judge〕, and his mother née Wang; both parents were living; his elder brother was Zhe and his younger brother Yuan, and he married a second wife, née Tu; he ranked 51st in the Henan Provincial Examination and 79th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Qing 劉清, courtesy name Yizhi, was from Dehua County, Jiujiang Prefecture, Jiangxi, registered in a military household; he was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, third in birth order, aged forty, and born on the tenth day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shouyi, his grandfather Ying, his father Gui, and his mother née Xiao; both parents were living; his elder brothers were Hong and Cheng, his younger brothers Ming and Qi, and his wife was née Zhou; he ranked 78th in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 173rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

張萬鍾，貫四川成都府資縣，軍籍，縣學生。治《詩經》，字公爵，行一，年三十六，二月二十八日生。曾祖元杲，祖琳，父永壽，母徐氏，繼母□氏。重慶下，弟萬鎰、萬銓。娶包氏。四川鄉試第三十三名，會試第二百十五名。

陳良佐，貫湖廣岳州府華容縣，民籍，國子生。治《易經》，字以忠，行四，年三十六，九月十九日生。曾祖壽祖，祖友富，父清〔冠帶監生〕，母鄭氏，繼母黎氏。永感下，兄良賢、良惠、良輔，弟良弼、良相。娶鄧氏。湖廣鄉試第七名，會試第二百七十六名。

汪瀅，貫直隸徽州府績溪縣，軍籍，國子生。治《書經》，字源潔，行三，年三十二，十一月初五日生。曾祖子通，祖友賢，父必清〔醫學訓科〕，母程氏，繼母方氏。嚴侍下，兄溥〔知州〕、淳，弟濟。娶程氏。應天府鄉試第一百十三名，會試第一百九十三名。
translation_en:
Liu Ji, registered in Linqing County, Dongchang Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a military household and was a county school student. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Yuheng. Fifth in birth order, he was aged twenty-six and was born on the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Jinyun, his grandfather Hai, and his father Guang; his legal mother was née Xu and his birth mother née Feng. His parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Ying, Jing, Xuan, and Zhang. He married a woman née Wang and subsequently a woman née Zhang. He ranked forty-eighth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 164th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Wanzhong, registered in Zi County, Chengdu Prefecture, Sichuan, belonged to a military household and was a county school student. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Gongjue. First in birth order, he was aged thirty-six and was born on the twenty-eighth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Yuangao, his grandfather Lin, and his father Yongshou; his mother was née Xu and his stepmother née □. His parents and grandparents were living. His younger brothers were Wanyi and Wanquan. He married a woman née Bao. He ranked thirty-third in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 215th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Liangzuo, registered in Huarong County, Yuezhou Prefecture, Huguang, belonged to a commoner household and was an Imperial University student. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Yizhong. Fourth in birth order, he was aged thirty-six and was born on the nineteenth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Shouzu, his grandfather Youfu, and his father Qing〔an Imperial University student granted the privilege of wearing official cap and girdle〕; his mother was née Zheng and his stepmother née Li. His parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Liangxian, Lianghui, and Liangfu, and his younger brothers Liangbi and Liangxiang. He married a woman née Deng. He ranked seventh in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 276th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Ying, registered in Jixi County, Huizhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a military household and was an Imperial University student. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Yuanjie. Third in birth order, he was aged thirty-two and was born on the fifth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Zitong, his grandfather Youxian, and his father Biqing〔Medical Instructor〕; his mother was née Cheng and his stepmother née Fang. His father was living and his mother deceased. His elder brothers were Pu〔Prefect〕 and Chun, and his younger brother Ji. He married a woman née Cheng. He ranked 113th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 193rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

His great-grandfather was Xiaoxian; his grandfather was Zhixue 〔Assistant Prefect〕; his father was Keming; his mother was née Zhu, and his stepmother’s surname is illegible. 劉聰〔貫直隸薊州衛，軍籍，江西宜春縣人，國子生，治《禮記》，字守愚，行一，年三十六，十月□□日生。〕曾祖德成，祖真，父能，母郭氏。重慶下，弟綱、紀、紳，娶錢氏。順天府鄉試第五名，會試第二百八十六名。

鄭惟桓〔貫順天府大興縣，富戶籍，浙江常山縣人，國子生，治《春秋》，字用文，行二十，年三十二，九月十一日生。〕曾祖善同〔義官〕，祖沂〔贈監察御史〕，父佑〔按察司副使〕，母徐氏〔封孺人〕。慈侍下，兄惟楠〔貢士〕、惟禎，弟惟樟、惟梓，娶□氏。順天府鄉試第七十名，會試第九十名。

孫司員〔貫浙江紹興府嵊縣，匠籍，縣學生，治《易經》，字宗規，行一，年二十九，七月初四日生。〕曾祖子實，祖純，父芳〔臨江府教授〕，母黃氏。具慶下，兄司方，弟司□、司温、司和，娶高氏。□□鄉試第八十七名，會試第一百六十名。
translation_en:
□□ (name illegible) was registered in a civilian household in … Zhen … Subprefecture, Zhili [?]. He was a student of the Directorate of Education and specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name began with Ting; the remainder and the following family-ranking information are unclear [?]. He was thirty-five, born on the thirtieth day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Wenxian 〔four illegible characters〕; his grandfather, Xian, was a District Magistrate; his father, Cong, held a prestige title; and his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were deceased. His younger brother was Shilong. He married a woman née Zhao and subsequently a woman née Peng. He ranked 114th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 111th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Cong was registered in a military household of Jizhou Guard, Zhili, and was a native of Yichun County, Jiangxi. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Record of Rites. His courtesy name was Shouyu, and he ranked first in his family. He was thirty-six, born on an illegible day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Decheng; his grandfather, Zhen; his father, Neng; and his mother, née Guo. His parents and grandparents were living. His younger brothers were Gang, Ji, and Shen. He married a woman née Qian. He ranked fifth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 286th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zheng Weihuan was registered in a wealthy household in Daxing County, Shuntian Prefecture, and was a native of Changshan County, Zhejiang. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Yongwen, and he ranked twentieth in his family. He was thirty-two, born on the eleventh day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather, Shantong, held the honorary title of Righteous Official; his grandfather, Yi, was posthumously appointed an Investigating Censor; his father, You, was a Surveillance Vice Commissioner; and his mother, née Xu, was granted the title of Lady (ruren). His father was deceased, and he attended his surviving mother. His elder brothers were Weinan, a tribute scholar (gongshi), and Weizhen; his younger brothers were Weizhang and Weizi. His wife's surname is illegible. He ranked seventieth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and ninetieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Sun Siyuan was registered in an artisan household in Sheng County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang. A student of the county Confucian school, he specialized in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Zonggui, and he ranked first in his family. He was twenty-nine, born on the fourth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Zishi; his grandfather, Chun; his father, Fang, was Director of the Linjiang Prefectural Confucian School; and his mother was née Huang. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Sifang; his younger brothers were Si□, Siwen, and Sihe. He married a woman née Gao. He ranked eighty-seventh in the Provincial Examination at an illegible location and 160th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
□□ Shou 綬, registered in an illegible county of Guangxin Prefecture, Jiangxi, was an additional student of the county Confucian school; two preceding characters are illegible [?]. He specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Yuqing; the following damaged text apparently gives his family birth order as seventeenth [?]. He was twenty-seven and was born on the second day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Yanjun; his grandfather, Du, was an Assistant Instructor; his father was Yu, and his mother was née Wang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Shen. He was betrothed to a woman née Zhou. He ranked sixty-third in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 244th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hong Yuan 洪遠, registered in a civilian household in She County, Huizhou Prefecture, in the directly administered region, was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Keyi, and he was third in family birth order, aged twenty-nine, born on the sixteenth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Zhang; his grandfather was Shou; his father, Kuan, was a Department Magistrate. His mother was née Wang [following character illegible]. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Da and Di, and his younger brother was Tong. He married a woman née Wu. He ranked 132nd in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 240th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hou Guan 侯觀, registered in a civilian household in Xiong County, Baoding Prefecture, in the directly administered region, was a Confucian scholar. He specialized in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Shibin, and he was third in family birth order, aged twenty-five, born on the eleventh day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Wenzhi. His grandfather, Lin, was a Treasury Commissioner, posthumously granted the title of Bureau Secretary. His father, Zan, was Chief Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments. His mother was née Wang [following character illegible], invested with the title Lady of Peace. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Tai and Yu; his younger brothers were Jie, Xun, and Yi. He married a woman née He. He ranked seventy-ninth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and thirty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Du Rong 杜榮, registered in a military household in an illegible locality of Datong Prefecture, Shanxi, was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name begins with Shi; the following two characters are illegible [?]. He was thirty-eight, born on the twenty-second day of the third month. His great-grandfather was □bi; his grandfather, Xian, was a Vice Commissioner of a Granary. The next two characters, apparently identifying his father, are illegible [?]; the official title given is Instructor in the Yin-yang School. His mother was née Song, and his stepmother was née Feng. His mother was living and his father deceased [final character of the formula illegible]. His younger brother was Hua. He married a woman née Lu. The examination ranking lines are damaged: the first surviving rank ends in “nineteen,” and the second in “hundred and sixteen”; the examinations and full ranks cannot be securely read [?].

translation_en:
Jiang Shuo, registered in □□□ [?], Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Wenzhao; he ranked second among his brothers, was thirty-six years old, and was born on the twenty-third day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Shisi, his grandfather Congli, and his father Yuan; his mother was née Wang and his stepmother née Zhuang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Cong, and his younger brothers were Rui and Long. He married a woman née Liu and subsequently another woman née Liu. He placed fifty-fifth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 321st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Huang Fuzheng, registered in Fushun County, Xuzhou Prefecture, Sichuan, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Classic of Documents. His courtesy name was Xianzhong; he ranked first among his brothers, was forty-eight years old, and was born on the sixth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Zhang, his grandfather Zhiqing, and his father Ji; his mother was née Pan. His father was living and his mother deceased. His younger brothers were Fuzhong, Fuzuo, and Fuyou. He married a woman née Xu. He placed sixty-fourth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 283rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tu Chou, registered in Fengcheng County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to an artisan household and was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Younian; he ranked second among his brothers, was forty years old, and was born on the seventeenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Renshou, his grandfather Zhibin, and his father Bingzhang; his mother was née Wu. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brother was Shou, and his younger brother Chou (幬). He married a woman née Zheng. He placed fourth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 231st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Chang, registered in Changshou County, Chongqing Prefecture, Sichuan, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Dalun; he ranked fourth among his brothers, was forty-five years old, and was born on the tenth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Xiang, his grandfather Shisheng, and his father Yixian, a Vice Commissioner of a granary. His legal mother and his birth mother were both née Yang. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brother was Shu, and his younger brothers were Chong and Ji. He married a woman née Yu. He placed fifty-second in the Provincial Examination of □□ [?] and 266th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yan □wen, courtesy name Yingkui, was registered in an illegible county in Huguang; his household registration category is also illegible [?]. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged twenty-seven, and born on the twenty-eighth day of the intercalary ninth month. His great-grandfather was □li, his grandfather Ji, and his father You, an honorary official for public benefactions; his mother was née Liu. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Jin, and his wife was née Liu. He ranked forty-fourth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 227th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Han Shaozong, courtesy name Yuhou, was registered in a civilian household in Chaoyi County, Tongzhou, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he was third in birth order, aged twenty-seven, and born on the eighteenth day of the intercalary ninth month. His great-grandfather was Gong, his grandfather Zisu, and his father Xian; his mother was née Zhang. His mother alone was living. His elder brothers were Zai and Jue, and his younger brothers Jizong, Xuzong, Shengzong, and Mianzong; his wife was née Yan. He ranked twentieth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and nineteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Daoning, courtesy name Yong’an, was registered in a military household in Guangshan County, Guangzhou, Runing Prefecture, Henan. A prefectural school student specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-four, and born on the ninth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Sicong, his grandfather Zhida, and his father Hao; his mother was née Chen. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Kuan, Fu, and Xian, and his wife was née Wang. He ranked forty-fourth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 169th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Xian, courtesy name Zhengang, was registered in a military household in Anyang County, Zhangde Prefecture, Henan. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he was fourth in birth order, aged thirty-three, and born on the twenty-fourth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Xianzhong, his grandfather Dacheng, and his father Xiang; his mother was née Wang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Hong, an official awaiting selection for appointment, Xian, and Xuan; his younger brothers were You, Shou, Yin, and Ning, and his wife was née Huangfu. He ranked twenty-ninth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 159th in the Metropolitan Examination.

A county school student specializing in the Book of Rites, he had the courtesy name Shizhi, ranked first in birth order, and was forty-two years old, born on the sixth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather’s and grandfather’s names are illegible; his father was Zan and his mother née Chen. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Shiji, Shimian, Shixi, Shizhong, and Shihe. He married a woman née Zhang and subsequently a woman née Zhao. His great-grandfather was Sili, his grandfather Yanling, and his father Ying, Associate Magistrate of a Department; his mother was née Wen. His mother alone was living. His courtesy name was Yuanyi; he ranked third in birth order and was thirty-eight years old, born on the first day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Delin, his grandfather Ying, and his father Jing, Commander of a Military Command; his mother was née Liu. His mother alone was living. His elder brothers were Tai and Zhen; his younger brothers were Ning and Yi, the latter an Instructor of Medicine. He married a woman née Li. He placed first in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 251st in the Metropolitan Examination.

His courtesy name was Dazhang; he ranked first in birth order and was thirty-six years old, born on the twenty-ninth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Zizhao, his grandfather Zhongcheng, his father Zonghao, and his mother née Zhang; both parents were living, his younger brothers were Yu and Xiang, and his wife was née Zhang; he placed seventy-sixth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 273rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ling Wenxian 凌文獻, registered in a civilian household in Sui’an County, Yanzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals; his courtesy name was Shixian, he ranked third among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-four, born on the sixth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Yongqing, his grandfather Yibang, his father Rengjun, and his mother née Yu; his father was deceased and his mother living, his elder brothers were Wengui and Wenkui, and his younger brothers Wentong and Wensheng; he married a woman née Zheng and subsequently a woman née Yu, and placed eighty-fourth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and sixty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Feng Gao 馮鎬, registered in a military household in Xinyang Subprefecture, Runing Prefecture, Henan, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Dajing, he ranked second among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-one, born on the nineteenth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Qing, his grandfather Jian, his father Youxin, his mother née Wan, and his stepmother née Lu; both parents were living, his elder brother was Zhao, his younger brothers Gang, Jin, and Zhong, and his wife was née Wang; he placed seventy-third in the Henan Provincial Examination and 143rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Gu Qiran 古其然, registered in a civilian household in Yongchuan County, Chongqing Prefecture, Sichuan, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Ticheng, he ranked seventh among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-eight, born on the ninth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Zhen’er, his grandfather Biqi, and his father Chu, a county Registrar; his father’s former wife was née Jiang and his mother née Deng; his father was deceased and his mother living, his elder brothers were Shangran, Haoran, Tianran, and Ziran, his younger brother Huoran, and his wife née Fang; he placed twenty-fifth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 137th in the Metropolitan Examination.

王佐〔貫山西遼州和順縣民籍，國子生，治易經，字廷輔，行一，年三十六，十月初三日生〕。曾祖貴，祖珍，父義〔巡檢〕，母張氏。具慶下，弟教、佩，娶馬氏。山西鄉試第六十四名，會試第一百三十六名。
translation_en:
Sun □ Jin [?], registered in an officer household of the Nanjing Palace Guard (Fujun Wei) and a native of Dong’an County, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Mingnan; he ranked second among his brothers, was forty years old, and was born on the twentieth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Boda, his grandfather Sheng, and his father Rang; his mother was née Liang and his stepmother née Han. His father was living. His elder brother was Duo and his younger brother Yue; his wife was née Xu. He placed 109th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 98th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Zuo, registered in a civilian household in Heshun County, Liaozhou, Shanxi, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Tingfu; he ranked first among his brothers, was thirty-six years old, and was born on the third day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Gui, his grandfather Zhen, and his father Yi, a Police Chief; his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Jiao and Pei; his wife was née Ma. He placed 64th in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 136th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en: The Emperor's decree reads: “We have heard that when the sage kings of the Three Dynasties transformed and perfected All-under-Heaven, each dynasty prized something in particular: the Xia prized loyalty, the Shang simplicity, and the Zhou refinement. Since their dynasties endured so long, can specific evidence of their achievements be cited and explained? Ever since humankind came into being, those speaking of consummate government have invariably cited Tang and Yu—the reigns of Yao and Shun—and the Three Dynasties. Yet here We speak only of the Three Dynasties without mentioning Tang and Yu. Does this mean that Tang and Yu alone had nothing they particularly prized…

translation_en:
The sagely and divine Emperor Gao □ [?] founded the great imperial enterprise, transformed barbarian ways into those of civilized China, restored the bonds of human relations, and once again set proper dress and headgear in order. Great indeed were his services to Heaven and Earth.

Emperor Wen, Taizong, succeeded to the imperial line and brought peace to the dynasty and the realm. Successive sage emperors further advanced government and moral instruction. 蓋萬古一道千聖一心豈孰謂帝王之致治有不同

體具於吾心其實用散於事物千聖由之而無外萬

punctuated:
臣曾彥。
臣對：臣聞帝王之致治則一道，帝王之行道則一心。蓋萬古一道，千聖一心，豈孰謂帝王之致治有不同道，而其行道有不同心者乎？道之大原出於天，其全體具於吾心，其實用散於事物，千聖由之而無外，萬古行之而無弊。但其繼世有治亂，而道不能無變同。繼治世者，道固不容於不同矣；繼亂世者，可容不變以救弊，而求歸於同者哉？若堯舜禹之禪受而無所變更，固同此道、同此心也；湯武之弔伐而有所損益，亦同此道、同此心也。漢唐宋之戡亂而治終不古若者，庸非此道此心有所未純，或善而不能守、弊而不能救者歟？然則有天下者，正心以端天下之本，行道以濟天下之用，則治可以興，弊可以救，俗尚可以移易，而囿斯世于皇極之中，追唐虞，躋三代，陋漢唐宋於不為，端在此矣。
臣惟皇帝陛下稟聰明睿智之資，備中正仁義之德，運乾剛而獨斷，普離明而畢照，遠宗帝王之道，近守祖宗之法。道已至而猶以為未至，治已臻而猶以為未臻，等于
translation_en:
Your servant, Zeng Yan.
Your servant replies: I have heard that emperors and kings bring about good government through one Way, and practice that Way with one mind. For throughout all ages there is one Way, and among a thousand sages there is one mind. Who could say that emperors and kings achieve good government through different Ways, or practice the Way with different minds? The great source of the Way issues from Heaven; its entirety is present in our minds, and its practical applications are distributed among affairs and things. A thousand sages follow it without going beyond it, and through all ages it is practiced without defect. Yet rulers succeed to ages of either order or disorder, and their application of the Way must therefore involve both change and continuity. Those succeeding to an orderly age surely cannot depart from the same Way; but could those succeeding to a disordered age refrain from making changes to remedy abuses and thereby seek a return to that same Way? When Yao, Shun, and Yu yielded and received the throne without making changes, they indeed shared this Way and this mind. When Tang and Wu consoled the afflicted and launched punitive campaigns, making reductions and additions, they too shared this Way and this mind. As for the Han, Tang, and Song, which quelled disorder yet ultimately failed to attain government equal to antiquity: was this not because their Way and mind were not wholly pure, or because they could not preserve what was good or remedy what was defective? Thus, if the possessor of All-under-Heaven rectifies his mind to set right the foundation of the realm, and practices the Way to meet its practical needs, good government can flourish, abuses can be remedied, and prevailing customs can be transformed. Bringing this age within the bounds of the August Ultimate, matching Tang and Yu, attaining the Three Dynasties, and disdaining to emulate the Han, Tang, and Song—all depend precisely upon this.
I reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor is endowed with intelligence and sagely wisdom, and possesses the virtues of centrality, rectitude, benevolence, and righteousness. You exercise the strength of Qian, Heaven, in making decisions alone, and spread the brightness of Li, Fire, to illuminate everything. Looking to the distant past, you take the Way of the emperors and kings as your model; looking to the nearer past, you uphold the laws of your ancestors. Though the Way has already reached perfection, you still consider it imperfect; though good government has already been attained, you still consider it unattained, equal to [?] …

translation_en:
…[six illegible characters] flourished still more. This, too, was like Shun’s succession to Yao [two illegible characters], following the same standard as Shun [?]. Your servant has reverently observed how, in the time of the sagely ancestor [?], instructions and admonitions were issued repeatedly, and imperial edicts, earnest and emphatic, were disseminated throughout the realm, as bright as the sun and stars. In teaching the people loyalty, he caused them to esteem integrity and a sense of shame and to strengthen the obligations of human relationships, abandoning their former harshness and meanness. In teaching the people simplicity, he caused them to cultivate trustworthiness and sincerity and practice frugality, abandoning their former presumptuous transgressions. In teaching the people refinement, he caused them to study rites and music and recite the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents, abandoning their former coarseness. This, too, shared Confucius’s intent in weighing what to remove and what to add; it certainly cannot be described as following a single fixed course. The Book of Documents says, “Great indeed are the king’s words!” It also says, “Undivided indeed is the king’s heart!” Your servant begs leave to offer these words in praise of the imperial ancestors. For the Way of our imperial ancestors is the Way of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, and Confucius; the heart of our imperial ancestors is the heart of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, and Confucius. Thus, for more than a hundred years, peace has prevailed within the seas. Their nurturing and gradual cultivation have penetrated flesh and marrow. Surely all the people of this age ought therefore to have followed their transforming influence.
Yet Your Majesty remains concerned that deceit and frequent litigation betray a lack of loyalty, that extravagance and exceeding one’s station betray a lack of simplicity, and that coarseness and disregard for ritual betray a lack of refinement. This surely reflects Your Majesty’s noble resolve, never complacent, seeking the Way as though it were not yet in sight. Yet people are born with desires. It is possible that, after a long period of peace, their inclinations have gradually gone astray; your servant, too, cannot guarantee that nothing accords with Your Majesty’s concerns. If we now wish to transform prevailing customs, eliminate their faults, and restore their simplicity, could there be any other way? To rectify the myriad people, one must begin by rectifying the hundred officials; to rectify the hundred officials, one must first rectify [twenty-four illegible characters]…

臣竊惟聖人未生，道在天地；聖人既生，道在聖人。堯舜，聖人也；禹湯文武，亦聖人也。堯舜相繼而為唐虞，聖聖相承，同守一道。斯時也，在官咸九德之俊乂，在野皆時雍之黎民。但見萬邦協和而已，政無可救之弊；但見四方風動而已，俗無可更之化。致治之迹，譬之元氣流行，渾渾噩噩，機緘莫測。後世雖欲強言其所尚，得邪？孔子曰：「大哉，堯之為君！蕩蕩乎，民無能名焉！」又曰：「無為而治者，其舜也歟！」正此謂也。

及乎禹繼舜而為夏，亦聖聖相承，同守一道。斯時也，猶有唐虞之遺風，而無可救之弊政。然當地平天成之後，事為漸繁之辰，政治之興，自不得不尚忠。忠者，渾然堅確之謂，未有形質之可指。如勞民以於□髮，泣囚至於下車，任工作貢，便隨所出以育上；錫土姓，□□隨□居而别□。凡典則之貽，率多出於忠誠。□□□□□□□□□□棄五□紀，威德作威，夏……

…[two illegible characters]. Your enlightened edict first asks about the prevailing customs of Tang and Yu, the Three Dynasties, and the Han, Tang, and Song, as well as why the people's customs today are not yet pure. It further charges us, your servants, to explain where action should begin. From this I know that Your Majesty desires to equal the glory of the Two Emperors and Three Kings and to exalt the great undertaking of your ancestors for all eternity. How could your servant fail to bow with clasped hands and knock his head upon the ground, acknowledging and extolling even a ten-thousandth part of your gracious command!

Your servant humbly considers that before the sages were born, the Way resided in Heaven and Earth; once the sages were born, the Way resided in them. Yao and Shun were sages; Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu were also sages. Yao and Shun succeeded one another as the rulers of Tang and Yu: sage succeeded sage, and both upheld the same Way. At that time, all those in office were outstanding men possessing the nine virtues, while all those outside office were common people living in harmony. One saw only the myriad states in concord; government had no abuses requiring remedy. One saw only the four quarters responding as if moved by the wind; customs required no further transformation. The workings of their good government resembled the circulation of primordial vital energy, whole and uncontrived, its inner mechanisms beyond fathoming. Even if later generations tried to specify what they esteemed, could they do so? Confucius said: “Great indeed was Yao as a ruler! So boundless was he that the people could find no name for it!” He also said: “Was it not Shun who governed through nonaction?” This is precisely what these sayings mean.

When Yu succeeded Shun and established the Xia, this too was one sage succeeding another and upholding the same Way. At that time, the inherited influence of Tang and Yu still endured, and there were no abuses in government requiring remedy. Yet after the earth had been brought to order and Heaven's work completed, as affairs gradually grew more numerous, the development of government necessarily came to emphasize wholehearted sincerity. Sincerity means being wholly steadfast and firm, without any tangible form that can be pointed out. Examples include his exertions for the people [the following wording concerning hair is damaged and unclear: ?]; his descending from his carriage to weep over prisoners; and his assigning services and establishing tribute, using what each locality produced to support the ruler. He granted lands and surnames [the following wording about residence and distinctions is damaged: ?]. The institutions and rules he handed down thus largely arose from wholehearted sincerity. …[?] had fallen into ruin. Tang could not [?] and attacked Xia, wishing to continue Yu’s former enterprise. Yet [?] correction [?], and institutions necessarily became progressively more detailed and gave priority to simplicity. Simplicity already possessed the framework of refinement, but still retained an intent of plainness. Thus, for the three pernicious customs and ten transgressions, [?] there were established punishments; for eight households and nine plots, fields had fixed boundaries. The ancestral temples had hymns, yet their wording remained simple; the grand carriage bore a falcon banner, yet its construction remained plain and sturdy. The plans and instructions handed down from that age mostly arose from this plainness. Thereafter, the dynasty’s sacrifices continued for six hundred years. Unfortunately, Zhou appeared: he treated the Five Phases with contempt and abandoned himself to drink and lust. The government of Shang then fell into utter ruin.
King Wu thus had no choice but to attack Zhou. Wishing to restore Shang’s former government and renew what had become tainted, he necessarily made institutions still more detailed and gave priority to refinement. Refinement meant that every affair displayed the brilliance of cultivated forms. Thus, he established twice as many offices as Xia and Shang, and in levying resources from the people combined the tribute and labor-assistance systems. He posthumously conferred royal status and added posthumous names to teach the people reverence; he established relations with the Yi peoples and assigned tribute obligations to demonstrate his authority to the people. The states, capitals, and outlying settlements received annual instruction, while the neighborhood units—the bi, lü, zu, and dang—were subject to seasonal prohibitions. Meritorious deeds were inscribed on the grand banner, and offenders were seated on the fine stone to mark their guilt. The regulations governing carriages, clothing, palaces, dwellings, implements, and utensils all specified in detail the distinctions of rank and dignity between superior and inferior, noble and humble. Truly, how splendid was its refinement! After many generations, however, the dynasty was unfortunately first brought to ruin under Kings You and Li, and further weakened under King Ping, until the achievement of the Zhou dynasty was swept away.
The institutions of the Three Kings were all good at their inception, but abuses arose as time passed. When a sage king arose and sought to correct imbalances and remedy abuses, he necessarily devised measures suited to the times. He never initially proclaimed to the multitude, “I wish to give priority to refinement, simplicity, or wholehearted sincerity.” Later people observed the differences and, finding that they seemed to follow this pattern, accordingly gave them these names [?]. Confucius said, “Yin followed the rites of Xia; what it subtracted and added can be known. 終而復始，□□□□，變極而必友，如晝夜之□□、寒暑之相□，乃道之當然也。惟聖人為能察其道之所在，而□以救弊。若周之衰，文極而弊，正當救之時也，而聖王不作，莫能救之。孔子有德無位，乃假魯史脩《春秋》，以寓一王之法。如商之爵三等，說者謂法天之三光，天道本下，親親而質省也；周之爵五等，說者謂法地之五行，地道敬上，尊尊而文煩也。《春秋》合伯、子、男為一也，辭無所貶，皆從子，曰夷進爵皆稱子，隱然寓改文從質之意。孔子不云：「大道之行，與三代之英，丘未之逮也，而有志焉。」他日答顏淵為邦之問曰：「行夏之時，乘殷之輅，服周之冕，樂則韶舞。」由是觀之，使聖人代周而王，其所損益可知矣。

奈何繼以嬴秦之強戾，破壞先王之法度，焚燒孔子之《六經》，而秦亦隨以亡矣。自秦而下，享國長久者，曰漢、曰唐、曰宋，皆以除暴禁亂，代虐以寬，有功於生民，故天下歸心焉。然詳諸君，不知正道之趨，惟就茍簡之政，百孔千瘡，隨補隨漏，又寧有定尚邪？董仲舒曰：「漢宜損周之文，用夏之忠。」亦循環之說也。漢高帝寬仁大度，而務為簡易；文帝恭儉節用，而示民敦朴，似忠。□□智術之多□□□，不免於雜霸，忠果安在？
translation_en:
…end and begin anew, [four illegible characters]; when change reaches its limit, it must return [?], just as day and night [two illegible characters] and cold and heat alternate [?]. This is the natural course of the Way. Only a sage can discern where the Way lies and [illegible character] remedy abuses. In Zhou’s decline, cultural refinement reached an extreme and produced abuses: precisely the moment when remedies were needed. Yet no sage king arose, and none could remedy them. Confucius possessed virtue but held no position of authority. He therefore drew upon the annals of Lu to compile the Spring and Autumn Annals, embodying in it the institutions of a true king. For example, Shang had three ranks of nobility. Commentators say these modeled Heaven’s three luminaries: Heaven’s Way is rooted below, cherishing kin and favoring plainness and simplicity. Zhou had five ranks of nobility. Commentators say these modeled Earth’s Five Phases: Earth’s Way reveres those above, honoring the honored and favoring elaborate cultural forms. The Spring and Autumn Annals treats earls, viscounts, and barons as one rank. Its wording implies no demotion; all follow the designation zi, or viscount. The passage concerning the Yi and advancement in rank likewise says that all are called zi [?]. This implicitly conveys the intention to replace elaborate forms with plainness. Did Confucius not say, “The practice of the Great Way and the outstanding men of the Three Dynasties—I, Qiu, did not live to witness them, yet I have a record of them”? On another occasion, answering Yan Yuan’s question about governing a state, he said, “Follow Xia’s calendar, ride in Yin’s carriage, wear Zhou’s ceremonial cap, and for music use the Shao dance.” From this we can see what a sage would have removed or added had he succeeded Zhou as king.

Alas, what followed was the violent perversity of Qin under the Ying house, which destroyed the former kings’ laws and institutions and burned Confucius’s Six Classics. Qin itself soon perished as well. After Qin, the dynasties that endured longest were Han, Tang, and Song. All eliminated violence and suppressed disorder, replacing tyranny with leniency and rendering service to the people; thus all under Heaven gave them their allegiance. Yet, examining these rulers closely, they did not know how to pursue the correct Way. They merely adopted makeshift policies: riddled with a hundred holes and a thousand sores, leaking again as soon as they were patched. How could they have had any settled guiding preference? Dong Zhongshu said, “Han should reduce Zhou’s cultural elaboration and employ Xia’s wholehearted sincerity.” This, too, is a theory of cyclical succession. Emperor Gao of Han was generous, humane, and magnanimous, striving for simplicity and ease. Emperor Wen was reverent and frugal, restrained expenditure, and showed the people an example of earnest plainness. This resembled wholehearted sincerity. [Two illegible characters] the profusion of clever stratagems [three illegible characters]—they could not avoid mixing in the methods of hegemonic rule. Where, then, was their wholehearted sincerity?

translation_en:
…[?] practiced benevolence and righteousness [?]. Xuanzong resolutely pursued diligence and frugality and fostered brotherly affection, coming close, perhaps, to unadorned simplicity. Yet there was much to be ashamed of among his blood relatives and within his household, and his rule did not escape disorder and barbarization [?]. Where, indeed, was that simplicity? Emperor Taizu of the Song employed Confucian ministers and abolished the regional military commands; Renzong appointed six scholars and attached importance to schools. Between ruler and ministers, favors and courtesies were elaborate and abundant; at court, deliberations were earnest and repeated. Through investigating rites and music and promoting and elucidating the Learning of the Way, they perhaps approached an esteem for cultural refinement. Yet deliberations were many and accomplishments few; false learning flourished while the Learning of the Way was prohibited. Where, then, was their cultural refinement? Cheng Yichuan said: “If a ruler is not hampered by the confused and mixed policies of later ages, his purpose will become settled and good government will be achieved.” The Han, Tang, and Song, limited as they were, had much that was confused and mixed. Your servant does not wish to recount it all tediously for Your Majesty, and knows, too, that Your Majesty’s aspirations do not lie in this direction.
I reverently reflect that Emperor Taizu Gao of our dynasty received Heaven’s luminous mandate and founded his great enterprise. He swiftly swept away the base customs of the foreign Yuan and greatly advanced the cultural brilliance of our illustrious age. He established the proper bonds of human relationships after their collapse and corruption, and restored Chinese dress after the era of robes fastened on the left. In remedying abuses, this was like Tang’s campaign against the Xia and King Wu’s campaign against the Shang, but his achievement was truly twice as great. Then our Emperor Taizong Wen brought order to the realm, and Emperor Renzong Zhao secured peace throughout the empire. Their achievements in continuing and carrying forward their predecessors’ work became ever greater, spreading moral instruction…

…[illegible] according to the land [illegible], everyone has the means of support, with nothing to regret in sustaining the living or burying the dead. This indeed assists in the work of [illegible]. As for the way to achieve good government, there must be words of the highest worth. When ministers of antiquity offered advice to their rulers, although some of it was worthy of adoption, it could not be free of shortcomings. Dong Zhongshu elucidated the Way of the Three Dynasties, and his learning [illegible] Heaven and humanity. His arguments had deep foundations and were rich in moral principle; his words grasped the constant principles of the sages’ Way. Chao Cuo submitted advice on military affairs, thinking carefully and comprehensively, exalting the ruler and restraining ministers, and speaking with vehement force. His arguments grasped the expedient application of the sages’ Way. Although Zhongshu grasped its constant principles, his statements about yin and yang, disasters, and anomalies could not avoid becoming far-fetched and impractical. Although Chao Cuo grasped its expedient application, his arguments concerning punishments and names and techniques of governance could not avoid becoming deceptive and improper. Thus, when the Song scholar Su Xun discussed these two men in the course of discussing Jia Yi, his assessment was surely fitting.

Jia Yi, talented though young, was summoned by Emperor Xiaowen. In his policy essay on orderly and secure government, one sees the utmost sincerity of loyalty and devotion. He urged the promotion of rites and music, understanding the foremost tasks of moral instruction; his language was eloquent. Zhang Liang, with his exceptional talents, assisted the rise of Emperor Gao. By devising strategies and determining plans, he quelled the great disorder of the realm; by offering loyal counsel as circumstances arose, he influenced its great affairs. His wisdom was comprehensive. Yet although Jia Yi’s arguments were eloquent, his cursory drafting of ceremonial rites and his proposals for the ‘three demonstrations and five baits’ showed insufficient care in his methods. Although Zhang Liang’s plans were wise, his methods rested on expedient stratagems and his learning followed Huang-Lao teachings, so his literary cultivation fell short. Thus, when the Song scholar Su Shi touched upon these two ministers in discussing Lu Zhi, his assessment was surely close to the truth.

Civil virtue, military achievement, famine relief, and bringing peace to the people [illegible]: these four tasks certainly deserve examination. Zhongshu, Chao Cuo, Jia Yi, and Zhang Liang: the limitations of these four ministers must likewise be understood. In a ruler’s selection of civil and military [personnel or measures?], he need not be bound by [illegible], but should employ what can be put into practice today. As for the way to bring peace and sustenance, [illegible] there must be means to benefit [illegible], and suitable men must be found to take charge of civil and military [illegible]…

陛下之心一於忠誠而智術之不用使朝廷之上懇乎忠
誠之相孚又擇忠誠之士以臨民而欺詐者必黜則
源清而流潔將見民皆讓畔於耕讓路於行縱有無
情者亦不得盡其辭矣尚何多訟之足慮乎
陛下之心務敦質朴而竒巧之不尚使朝廷之上淳乎質
朴之相倣又擇質朴之士以養民而貪墨者必罪則
表正而影端將見民皆務本節用量入為出縱有好
侈者亦必革其心矣尚何僭踰之足慮乎
陛下之心崇乎禮文而苟簡之不形使朝廷之上秩然禮
===
文之相接又擇有禮而文者以教民而鄙陋者必去
則身教者從將見民皆興於禮而進退揖讓之有節
冠昏喪祭之有儀所謂非禮無為也尚何粗鄙之足
慮乎忠也質也文也以之相用而不偏廢以之相濟
而不偏重上行而下效世守而不失則可以躋斯世

皇極之中矣而曷嘗不自
聖心中來邪蓋有此心則有此道有此道則有此治有此
治則有此效理之必然也故臣之愚必以為致治惟

陛下之心務敦質朴，而竒巧之不尚，使朝廷之上淳乎質朴之相倣，又擇質朴之士以養民，而貪墨者必罪，則表正而影端，將見民皆務本節用，量入為出，縱有好侈者，亦必革其心矣。尚何僭踰之足慮乎？
陛下之心崇乎禮文，而苟簡之不形，使朝廷之上秩然禮文之相接，又擇有禮而文者以教民，而鄙陋者必去，則身教者從，將見民皆興於禮，而進退揖讓之有節，冠昏喪祭之有儀，所謂非禮無為也。尚何粗鄙之足慮乎？忠也，質也，文也，以之相用而不偏廢，以之相濟而不偏重，上行而下效，世守而不失，則可以躋斯世於皇極之中矣。而曷嘗不自聖心中來邪？蓋有此心則有此道，有此道則有此治，有此治則有此效，理之必然也。故臣之愚必以為致治惟□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□
translation_en:
If Your Majesty’s heart is devoted wholly to loyalty and sincerity, employing no cunning devices, so that those at court earnestly trust one another in loyalty and sincerity; and if you also choose loyal and sincere men to govern the people, invariably dismissing the deceitful, then the source will be clear and the stream pure. You will see the people yield the boundaries of their fields to others when ploughing and give way to others on the road. Even those whose claims lack substance will be unable to press their pleadings to the full. What further cause will there be to fear excessive litigation?

If Your Majesty’s heart strives to foster simplicity and plainness, esteeming no clever artifices, so that those at court sincerely emulate one another in simplicity and plainness; and if you also choose simple and upright men to nurture the people, invariably punishing the corrupt, then the gnomon will be upright and its shadow straight. You will see the people devote themselves to the fundamental occupation of agriculture, economize in their expenditures, and keep their spending within their income. Even those fond of extravagance will assuredly reform their hearts. What further cause will there be to fear transgressions of rank and station?

If Your Majesty’s heart esteems ritual and refinement, allowing no careless shortcuts to appear, so that those at court deal with one another in an orderly manner through ritual and refinement; and if you also choose men possessed of ritual propriety and refinement to instruct the people, invariably removing the uncouth, then those taught by personal example will follow it. You will see the people all stirred to practice ritual, observing due measure in advancing and withdrawing, bowing and yielding precedence, and proper forms in capping ceremonies, marriages, funerals, and sacrifices. This is what is meant by doing nothing contrary to ritual propriety. What further cause will there be to fear coarseness and vulgarity? Loyalty, simplicity, and refinement should work together, with none neglected, and complement one another, with none given excessive weight. If those above practice them and those below emulate them, and they are preserved through the generations without loss, this age can be raised to the central standard of the August Ultimate. And how could this ever fail to originate in Your Majesty’s sagely heart? For where there is this heart, there is this Way; where there is this Way, there is this government; and where there is this government, there are these results. This necessarily follows from principle. Thus your servant, in his humble understanding, firmly holds that achieving good government depends solely on [twenty-two illegible characters]…

也人有是形莫不有是心一心之微眾欲攻之
不能全其體以擴其用者多矣所以持是心使不為
利欲所昏楛其要又在於敬乎敬者聖學之所以成
始成終者也堯之允恭舜之恭己禹之祗德湯之聖
敬文王之敬止武王之肅將凡聖人之持心必自敬
始易所謂乾乾書所謂精一詩所謂思無邪禮所謂
毋不敬凡聖經之垂訓未始不丁寧於此也伏望
陛下靜而敬以存養此心之體動而敬以省察此心之用
不貳以二不參以三不東以西不南以北
大廷如是深宮如是大政大事如是微言細行如是使
===
人欲日淨天理日明則心無不正而道從此出由是
應事而事無不當由是處物而物無不宜民生由是
而益厚風俗由是而益醇華夏蠻貊由是而益率俾
四時五行由是而益順序五岳四海由是而益效靈
曠世之祥諸福之物由是而無不臻矣此則臣之所
拳拳深望於
陛下者
陛下策臣等而於篇終有曰子諸生明經待問久矣茲欲
造于廷詳著以獻朕將親覽焉其所以期待臣等可

punctuated:
也。人有是形，莫不有是心。一心之微，眾欲攻之，不能全其體以擴其用者多矣。所以持是心，使不為利欲所昏楛，其要又在於敬乎！敬者，聖學之所以成始成終者也。堯之允恭，舜之恭己，禹之祗德，湯之聖敬，文王之敬止，武王之肅將，凡聖人之持心，必自敬始。《易》所謂乾乾，《書》所謂精一，《詩》所謂思無邪，《禮》所謂毋不敬，凡聖經之垂訓，未始不丁寧於此也。伏望陛下靜而敬，以存養此心之體；動而敬，以省察此心之用。不貳以二，不參以三，不東以西，不南以北。大廷如是，深宮如是，大政大事如是，微言細行如是，使人欲日淨，天理日明，則心無不正，而道從此出。由是應事，而事無不當；由是處物，而物無不宜。民生由是而益厚，風俗由是而益醇，華夏蠻貊由是而益率俾，四時五行由是而益順序，五岳四海由是而益效靈，曠世之祥、諸福之物，由是而無不臻矣。此則臣之所拳拳深望於陛下者。
陛下策臣等，而於篇終有曰：「子諸生明經待問久矣，茲欲造于廷，詳著以獻，朕將親覽焉。」其所以期待臣等，可謂
