… All people who possess this human form possess this heart-and-mind. Subtle as this single mind is, it is assailed by a multitude of desires; many therefore fail to preserve its substance intact and extend its functioning. Is not reverent attentiveness, then, the essential means of maintaining this mind and keeping it from being clouded and impaired [?] by desires for gain? Reverent attentiveness is what brings the learning of the sages to fulfillment from beginning to end. Yao’s true reverence, Shun’s reverent bearing, Yu’s reverence for virtue, Tang’s sagely reverence, King Wen’s abiding in reverence, and King Wu’s reverent carrying forward of his charge—all show that the sages invariably began with reverent attentiveness in maintaining their minds. What the Book of Changes calls unceasing diligence, the Book of Documents calls refinement and singleness, the Book of Odes calls having no wayward thoughts, and the Book of Rites calls being reverent in everything: the instructions handed down in the sages’ classics have never ceased to insist earnestly upon this.
I humbly hope that Your Majesty will remain reverently attentive in stillness, preserving and nourishing the substance of this mind, and reverently attentive in activity, examining its functioning. Do not let a second concern divide it in two, or a third divide it in three; do not turn eastward attention westward, or southward attention northward. Be thus in the great court and in the inner palace, in great policies and great affairs, and in the smallest words and actions. Let human desires be cleared away day by day and heavenly principle become clearer day by day. Then the mind will be entirely rectified, and the Way will issue from it. Responding to affairs through this, nothing will be handled improperly; dealing with things through this, nothing will be treated inappropriately. The people’s livelihood will thereby become more abundant, customs more sincere, and the peoples of Huaxia and the Man and Mo ever more obedient [?]. The four seasons and the Five Phases will proceed ever more regularly in their proper order; the Five Sacred Peaks and the Four Seas will increasingly manifest their numinous efficacy. Auspicious signs unseen for generations and all things bearing blessings will without exception arrive. This is what your servant earnestly and profoundly hopes for from Your Majesty.
In putting a policy question to us, Your Majesty said at its conclusion: “You students have long elucidated the classics and awaited questioning. What I have studied in ordinary times is the Way of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu; what I have sought to understand are the canonical texts of Changes, Documents, Odes, Rites, Music, and Spring and Autumn Annals. My earnest devotion to my sovereign and love of my country have long been nurtured in this way. Today, fortunate to offer this response before Your Majesty, I dare not distort citations or indulge in vague explanations. I have respectfully set forth the essentials of the teachings of the mind transmitted by the Two Emperors and Three Kings and embodied in the Six Classics, offering them at the close of this essay. 臣對臣聞有治天下之大道有治天下之大法夫道
莫大乎中也古之帝王所以治天下者不出乎此而
其致治之法亦維持乎此而已唐虞之治其道如一
而法無損益故無所異尚三代之治其道相因而法
有損益故各有所尚治雖不同而同歸於一中也若
漢若唐若宋不得乎道之中而其為法無有定尚此

必行帝王之大道舉帝王之大法因時救敝而一歸

臣楊守阯。

臣對：臣聞，有治天下之大道，有治天下之大法。夫道莫大乎中也，古之帝王所以治天下者不出乎此，而其致治之法亦維持乎此而已。唐虞之治，其道如一，而法無損益，故無所異尚；三代之治，其道相因，而法有損益，故各有所尚。治雖不同，而同歸於一中也。若漢、若唐、若宋，不得乎道之中，而其為法無有定尚，此唐虞三代之治所以非漢唐宋之能及也。有天下者，必行帝王之大道，舉帝王之大法，因時救敝，而一歸乎中，則治隆俗美，將復見唐虞三代之盛，而區區漢唐宋風斯下矣。欽惟皇帝陛下，以天縱之資，履大寳之位，緝熈聖學，總攬乾綱。所講讀者皆二帝三王之書，所體行者皆二帝三王之道，所設施者皆二帝三王之法。十五年間，孜孜宵旰，必欲儷美乎唐虞三代之治。兹者復進臣等，策之於廷，首及唐虞三代以來治化之所尚，於以今日移風易俗、推行之所始，皆非愚臣所能及也。然臣自幼學，竊嘗誦帝王之遺經，求帝王之治道，欲以致吾君如二帝三王，濟斯世如唐虞三代也。但恐無階以進，有志未遂，今幸
translation_en:
Your servant, Yang Shouzhi.

Your servant replies: I have heard that there is a great Way for governing All under Heaven and that there are great methods for governing All under Heaven. Nothing in the Way is greater than the Mean. The means by which the emperors and kings of antiquity governed All under Heaven never departed from this, and their methods for achieving good government likewise served only to uphold it. Under Tang and Yu, the Way of government was one and the same, and its methods underwent neither subtraction nor addition; thus there was no difference in what they esteemed. Under the Three Dynasties, the Way was inherited from one to the next, while the methods underwent subtraction and addition; thus each had its own emphasis. Although their governments differed, they all converged upon the single Mean. The Han, Tang, and Song, however, failed to attain the Mean of the Way, and their methods had no settled guiding emphasis. This is why the Han, Tang, and Song could not equal the government of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. Whoever possesses All under Heaven must practice the great Way of the ancient emperors and kings and put their great methods into effect, remedying abuses according to the needs of the times and bringing everything back to the Mean. Government will then flourish and customs become admirable. The splendor of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties will be seen again, and the modest achievements of the Han, Tang, and Song will fall below it.

I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor, endowed by Heaven, has ascended the imperial throne, continually advanced and illuminated your sagely learning, and held supreme authority in your grasp. What you study and read are all the writings of the Two Emperors and Three Kings; what you embody and practice is their Way; what you institute and implement are their methods. For fifteen years you have labored diligently, working late into the night and delaying your meals, determined to match the excellence of the government of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. Now you have again summoned us, your servants, to answer policy questions at court. You begin with what was esteemed in government and moral transformation from Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties onward, and proceed to where one should begin today in transforming customs and putting these principles into practice. All this lies beyond the reach of your ignorant servant.

Yet from my earliest schooling, I have ventured to recite the classical writings bequeathed by the ancient emperors and kings and to seek their Way of government, wishing thereby to bring my sovereign to the stature of the Two Emperors and Three Kings and to succor this age as in the days of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. I feared only that I had no avenue by which to advance, and my aspiration remained unfulfilled. Now, fortunately …

translation_en:
…□□, one of the lowliest commoners clad in plain cloth, whose words, humble as those of a grass-cutter or wood-gatherer, have reached Your Majesty’s hearing behind the embroidered screen. Truly, this is the time to speak again [?]. Dare your servant fail to exhaust whatever small insight his foolish deliberations may yield, in answering even one ten-thousandth of Your sacred inquiry?
Your servant has heard that the august Supreme Lord bestowed an upright nature upon the people. Its three great bonds are those between ruler and minister, father and son, and husband and wife; its five constant principles are benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness. Each assuredly has its proper standard: this is what is called the Mean inherently present in nature. Yet people are born with desires, and few can accord with the Mean. An emperor or king must therefore arise to carry on Heaven’s work and establish the supreme standard—as Yao, Shun, and Yu held fast to the Mean, Tang established the Mean, King Wen reverently abided in his proper resting place, and King Wu established the supreme standard. Only then can all the people under Heaven be brought to follow the Mean of this Way. This is the great Way by which emperors and kings govern all under Heaven. Yet to bring forth good government through the Way, there must be methods to support it. Thus they instituted rites, music, punishments, and administration, and established institutions, ordinances, and standards, to sustain this Way and set bounds for the people, so that they would neither go too far nor fall short. These are the great methods of governing all under Heaven.
The Way is what all ages follow; methods are curtailed or supplemented according to the times. When the course of the world flourishes and one age of good government succeeds another, what is followed remains unchanged, and the methods of government need no curtailment or supplementation. How, then, could there be different preferences? But when the course of the world gradually declines and order and disorder succeed one another, what is followed may be lost, and the methods of government cannot escape curtailment or supplementation. How could there fail to be differing preferences for sincerity, simplicity, and refinement? What is called sincerity is an undivided wholeness of truthfulness and firmness, before simplicity can even be spoken of. With simplicity, definite forms and arrangements gradually emerge, but refinement has not yet been reached. With refinement, embellishment is added in every matter to the existing institutions. These were not names people established for themselves at the time; later generations observed how things had been and named them accordingly.
Consider, moreover, the ages of Tang and Yu. Their rulers were Yao and Shun. Their ministers were Yu, Gao Yao, Ji, and Xie, together with the Four Chiefs and the Nine Ministers, united in reverence and harmonious respect. Their…

text:
□□□以睦五典克從也故建官惟百而其官
制同矣五禮明備而其禮制同矣曆象以授時璣衡
以齊政而其敬天勤民又同矣罪疑惟輕功疑惟重
刑賞忠厚之至也而孰尚乎忠茅茨土階陶尊瓦𤬛
制度質朴之至也而孰尚乎質煥乎文章五采作服
此又其文之著也而孰尚乎文故堯在位七十載而
民相忘於不識不知之天舜在位三十三載而民相
安於無為而治之域其無所尚也如此孔子曰堯舜
垂衣裳而天下治董仲舒曰堯舜相受而守一道無
捄敝之政也以是觀之則唐虞之治豈外乎一中也

…[three illegible characters] thereby were in harmony, and the five norms of human relationships were duly observed. Thus, they established only a hundred offices, and their official institutions were alike. The five rites were clearly and fully provided for, and their ritual institutions were alike. They observed and calculated the celestial movements to announce the seasons, and used the jade celestial instrument and its sighting tube to bring the heavenly motions into order; their reverence for Heaven and diligence on behalf of the people were likewise the same. When guilt was doubtful, they chose the lighter punishment; when merit was doubtful, they chose the greater reward. This was the utmost sincerity and generosity in punishment and reward: which of them particularly exalted sincerity? Thatched roofs, earthen steps, earthenware wine vessels, and pottery jars represented the utmost simplicity in their institutions: which of them particularly exalted simplicity? Their cultural forms shone brilliantly, and the five colors were used to make ceremonial robes. Here, too, their refinement was manifest: which of them particularly exalted refinement? Thus, during Yao’s seventy years on the throne, the people lived together oblivious to rule, in a world requiring neither conscious recognition nor knowledge. During Shun’s thirty-three years on the throne, the people lived together in peace in a realm governed through nonaction. Such was their absence of any particular preference. Confucius said: “Yao and Shun let their robes hang down, and all under Heaven was governed.” Dong Zhongshu said: “Yao and Shun succeeded one another and maintained a single Way; they had no policies for remedying abuses.” Viewed in this light, could the government of Tang and Yu have departed from the one mean?

Speaking of the Three Dynasties, Xia inherited Shun’s good government, and the enduring human relationships were duly ordered. At that time, prevailing customs were sincere and steadfast; adapting to what suited the age, Xia exalted sincerity. Shang inherited the disorder of Jie and began restoring the norms of human relationships. At that time, prevailing customs were gradually opening up; to remedy the abuses arising from sincerity, Shang exalted simplicity. Zhou inherited the disorder of Zhou 紂 and gave weight to the five teachings for the people. At that time, human culture was becoming increasingly manifest; to remedy the abuses arising from simplicity, Zhou exalted refinement. Thus, in governing the people, Xia put emoluments before the exercise of authority, Shang put punishments before rewards, and Zhou honored ritual and prized generosity. In establishing ritual, Xia had five rites; Shang had six rites and seven teachings; and Zhou had three hundred ceremonial rules and three thousand rules of deportment. In the same rite of laying out the coffin before burial, Xia placed it at the eastern steps, Shang between the two pillars, and Zhou above the western steps, thereby embodying the respective intentions of sincerity, simplicity, and refinement. …[Two illegible characters] there are remedies supplied by loyalty, simplicity, and refinement. Thus, during the Xia’s four hundred years, the people’s ways were largely honest and plain; during the Shang’s six hundred years, extravagant and wasteful customs were rare among the people; and during the Zhou’s eight hundred years, the people advanced daily toward cultural refinement. Such were the respective values they esteemed. Confucius said: “The Yin followed the rites of the Xia; what they subtracted and added can be known. The Zhou followed the rites of the Yin; what they subtracted and added can be known.” Dong Zhongshu said: “The Xia esteemed loyalty, the Shang esteemed reverence, and the Zhou esteemed refinement. These are what must be employed to remedy the failings of the preceding dynasty.” Viewed in this light, how could the government of the Three Dynasties have departed from the single principle of the Mean? Yet changes, ancient and modern, must reverse when they reach their extreme, just as day and night give rise to one another and cold and heat alternate. Thus Sima Qian said: “The Xia governed through loyalty. When loyalty deteriorated, petty people became uncouth; hence the Shang succeeded them with reverence. When reverence deteriorated, petty people became preoccupied with spirits; hence the Zhou succeeded them with refinement. When refinement deteriorated, petty people became insincere; hence nothing remedies insincerity better than loyalty. The Way of the Three Kings moves as if in a cycle, ending and beginning again.” His account is correct.

Yet at the end of the Zhou, refinement had deteriorated, and this was a time when change was needed. No sage king arose, however, and no one could effect change and restore sound governance as Sima Qian described. At that time, even a sage such as Confucius could not attain the position of emperor or king. He therefore composed the Spring and Autumn Annals to embody the laws of true kingship. In the commentary on Hu of Zheng’s flight into exile, Gongyang speaks of treating earls, viscounts, and barons as one rank. Zheng Xuan and He Xiu accordingly held that the Shang had three ranks of nobility and the Zhou five, and that the Spring and Autumn Annals combined earls, viscounts, and barons into a single rank, making three ranks together with dukes and marquises. This, they held, meant changing the Zhou’s refinement and adopting the Shang’s simplicity. Now, replacing refinement with simplicity was indeed what the times required, and certainly accorded with the principle of cyclical change. Yet some have already criticized the error in the claim that earls, viscounts, and barons formed a single rank; others have likewise refuted the claim that the Shang had three ranks of nobility. As for the composition of the Spring and Autumn Annals, it is what Master Cheng called the great law that remains unchanged through a hundred kings, the proper mean between refinement and simplicity. …[?] the apocryphal commentaries on the Spring and Autumn Annals. The claim that honoring the exalted and cherishing one’s kin follows the Way of Heaven, while refinement and honoring the exalted follow the Way of Earth, comes instead from the apocryphal commentaries on the Classic of Music. The claim that dynasties favoring simplicity had three ranks of nobility, modeled on Heaven’s three luminaries, whereas dynasties favoring refinement had five ranks, modeled on Earth’s Five Phases, also comes from the apocryphal commentaries on the Spring and Autumn Annals. These accounts have long been transmitted by scholars of the two Han dynasties; some need not be debated exhaustively. It is only regrettable that Confucius’s Way was not put into practice during the Spring and Autumn period. Consequently, conditions in the world deteriorated ever further, until the Qin entirely destroyed the laws of the former kings and devoted itself exclusively to harsh and crude government.
When the Han arose, it removed the abuses [?] of Qin and set the main framework of government right, but could not yet transform its governance. Dong Zhongshu said that, because the Han succeeded an age of great disorder, it should somewhat reduce Zhou refinement and bring Xia sincerity into effective use. This, too, was an account of cyclical change. Qin had already entirely abolished Zhou refinement, and Han subsequently began gradually to employ Xia sincerity. Yet Zhongshu still spoke thus precisely because he meant that Zhou refinement should not be wholly altered, but only somewhat reduced, and that Xia sincerity should be employed to the fullest—hence his words “bring into effective use.” Yet the rites rehearsed with cords and bundles of reeds incorporated Qin ceremonial, while efforts to consult antiquity were obstructed by the teachings of Huangdi and Laozi. Where, then, was Zhou refinement ever present? Only its generous government, which allowed the people respite and recovery, and its wholesome moral influence, which nearly made punishments unnecessary, bore some resemblance to Xia sincerity.
When the Tang arose, it took warning from Sui harshness and cruelty and favored benevolence and generosity in its methods of government. Later, some favored penal administration, others literary composition, and policies changed repeatedly. Yet although the myriad particulars were attended to, the main framework was not correct. How could government that borrowed the guise of benevolence and mingled barbarian practices compare with the sincerity and simplicity of the former kings? When the Song arose [?], it took warning from the cruelty of the Five Dynasties and favored sincerity and generosity in its methods of government. Later, some favored the Learning of the Way, others the New Policies, and there was unsettled contention. Yet although the main framework was correct, the myriad particulars remained unattended to. How could its prohibitions against “treacherous factions” and “false learning” compare with the simplicity and refinement of the former kings? text:
善治也自宋之衰胡元穢夏亂常瀆倫為天
地開闢以來所無之大變天厭夷德命我
太祖高皇帝以聖智之資神武之界革百年之虜運開萬
世之洪圖惟中國帝王所自立天所以制夷狄也彼
惡得而亂之我
太祖恢復中夏而承帝王之正統五典天之所敘帝王所
惇也彼惡得而瀆之我
太祖重脩人紀以正天地之常經五禮天之所秩帝王所
庸也彼惡得而壞之我
太祖申明禮義以復中國之冠裳此其因革之大者是大
===
有功於天地有功於帝王也由是
□宗文皇帝繼之而中靖邦家
仁宗昭皇帝繼之而厚培邦本
宣宗章皇帝又繼之而丕闡宏猷
英宗睿皇帝又繼之而重光盛烈
列聖相承一以綱常為治其道即帝王之道其法即帝王
之法百餘年來四海之內漸被仁義之澤深且厚矣
夫孰能名其所尚哉孟以為忠也而又兼乎質以為
質也而又兼乎文姑舉其一二言之如圜丘歲祀惟
以時行用敬天也籍田之制勸力本也里

punctuated: 善治也。自宋之衰，胡元穢夏，亂常瀆倫，為天地開闢以來所無之大變。天厭夷德，命我太祖高皇帝以聖智之資、神武之界，革百年之虜運，開萬世之洪圖。惟中國，帝王所自立，天所以制夷狄也，彼惡得而亂之？我太祖恢復中夏，而承帝王之正統。五典，天之所敘，帝王所惇也，彼惡得而瀆之？我太祖重脩人紀，以正天地之常經。五禮，天之所秩，帝王所庸也，彼惡得而壞之？我太祖申明禮義，以復中國之冠裳。此其因革之大者，是大有功於天地，有功於帝王也。由是，□宗文皇帝繼之而中靖邦家，仁宗昭皇帝繼之而厚培邦本，宣宗章皇帝又繼之而丕闡宏猷，英宗睿皇帝又繼之而重光盛烈。列聖相承，一以綱常為治，其道即帝王之道，其法即帝王之法。百餘年來，四海之內，漸被仁義之澤，深且厚矣。夫孰能名其所尚哉？孟以為忠也，而又兼乎質；以為質也，而又兼乎文。姑舉其一二言之，如圜丘歲祀，惟以時行，用敬天也；籍田之制，勸力本也；里
translation_en:
…good government. From the decline of the Song, the barbarian Yuan defiled the Chinese realm, disrupted the constant moral principles, and profaned human relationships—a calamity unprecedented since Heaven and Earth first opened. Heaven, disgusted with barbarian virtue, commissioned our Emperor Gao, Taizu, endowed with sagely wisdom and divine martial prowess [?], to overthrow a century of barbarian rule and inaugurate a grand enterprise for ten thousand generations. The Central Realm is where emperors and kings establish themselves, and through it Heaven controls the barbarians. How could they be permitted to throw it into disorder? Our Taizu restored the Chinese realm and inherited the legitimate succession of emperors and kings. The five moral relationships are ordered by Heaven and cultivated by emperors and kings. How could they be permitted to profane them? Our Taizu restored the norms of human relationships, thereby rectifying the constant principles of Heaven and Earth. The five categories of rites are ranked by Heaven and employed by emperors and kings. How could they be permitted to destroy them? Our Taizu clarified ritual and righteousness, restoring the caps and robes of the Central Realm. These were the great instances of his preservation and reform: through them he rendered great service to Heaven and Earth and to emperors and kings.

Thereafter, Emperor Wen, □zong, succeeded him and brought peace within the realm; Emperor Zhao, Renzong, succeeded him and firmly strengthened the foundations of the state; Emperor Zhang, Xuanzong, succeeded in turn and greatly expanded the grand design; and Emperor Rui, Yingzong, succeeded in turn and renewed the radiance of their magnificent achievements. The successive sage rulers governed consistently through the cardinal bonds and constant moral principles. Their Way was precisely the Way of emperors and kings; their methods were precisely those of emperors and kings. For more than a hundred years, all within the Four Seas have gradually received the blessings of benevolence and righteousness, deep and abundant indeed. Who could name the particular quality they esteem? If one calls it loyalty [?], it also embraces simplicity; if one calls it simplicity, it also embraces refinement. Let us mention just one or two examples: the annual sacrifice at the Circular Mound is performed at its appointed season to show reverence for Heaven; the institution of the imperial ploughing field encourages devotion to agriculture, the fundamental occupation; the village [?]…

text:
專之年也其敬天勤民可謂忠矣祀宣聖以
神主而復淳古之規正嶽瀆以本名而革侈美之號
水精宮漏立命碎之鏤金之床即命毀之其議禮制
度可謂質矣朝覲會同粲粲乎玉帛之儀庠序學校
洋洋乎絃歌之聲考正韻書而百代之大音始完表
章經傳而斯文之大全始備其典章文物可謂文矣
三者皆得乎中而不可以一偏名之誠若唐虞之無

專之年也。其敬天勤民，可謂忠矣。祀宣聖以神主，而復淳古之規；正嶽瀆以本名，而革侈美之號。水精宮漏，立命碎之；鏤金之床，即命毀之。其議禮制度，可謂質矣。朝覲會同，粲粲乎玉帛之儀；庠序學校，洋洋乎絃歌之聲。考正韻書，而百代之大音始完；表章經傳，而斯文之大全始備。其典章文物，可謂文矣。三者皆得乎中，而不可以一偏名之，誠若唐虞之無所尚也。
承平日久，不能無敝。天下之民化於忠，而篤實者眾矣。然而姦宄萌生，狡偽百態，鼠牙雀角，獄訟繁興，其情猶或有變詐而多訟者焉。化於質，而儉約者眾矣。然而富人大賈，墻屋繡文；貴戚豪門，犬馬粱肉。其用猶或有奢靡而踰分者焉。化於文，而興禮義者眾矣。然而學校之教，或尚虛文；都鄙之氓，相沿陋習。其俗之粗鄙而鮮禮者，亦或有之。是宜上廑宸衷，而欲去敝易俗，囿民於皇極之中也。
臣以為，陛下欲囿民於皇極之中，必先盡皇極之道。皇極之道無他，即堯舜禹湯文武以及□之□
translation_en:
…the year [?]. Such reverence for Heaven and diligence on behalf of the people may be called sincerity. In sacrificing to Confucius, the Sage Who Proclaims the Teaching, a spirit tablet was used, restoring the unadorned practices of antiquity. The sacred mountains and waterways were designated by their original names, abolishing their extravagantly laudatory titles. The crystal palace clepsydra was immediately ordered smashed; the bed ornamented with carved gold was at once ordered destroyed. Such deliberation over ritual and establishment of institutions may be called simplicity. At court audiences and assemblies, the ceremonies involving jade and silk were resplendent; in the schools, the sounds of strings and singing rang out abundantly. Through examining and correcting rhyme books, the great sounds transmitted through a hundred generations were at last made complete; through honoring and elucidating the Classics and their commentaries, the full heritage of this culture was at last comprehensively furnished. Such institutions and cultural accomplishments may be called refinement. All three attained the proper mean, so that no single tendency can characterize them. Truly, this resembles the age of Tang and Yu, which gave exclusive preference to none.
Yet prolonged peace cannot be free from abuses. Among the people of the realm, many have been transformed by sincerity and become earnest and honest. Nevertheless, wrongdoing emerges, cunning and deceit take a hundred forms, and quarrels—like the proverbial rat’s teeth and sparrow’s horn—give rise to proliferating lawsuits. In their dispositions, some thus remain deceitful and litigious. Many have been transformed by simplicity and become frugal and restrained. Nevertheless, wealthy men and great merchants adorn their walls and houses with embroidered patterns, while imperial relatives and powerful households feed their dogs and horses fine grain and meat. In their expenditure, some thus remain extravagant and exceed the bounds of their station. Many have been transformed by refinement and promote ritual propriety and righteousness. Nevertheless, instruction in the schools sometimes prizes empty ornament, while people in the cities and countryside perpetuate vulgar habits. Some thus still have coarse customs and little sense of propriety. These matters fittingly trouble Your Majesty’s heart and move you to wish to eliminate abuses, reform customs, and bring the people within the supreme imperial standard.
Your servant believes that, if Your Majesty wishes to bring the people within the supreme imperial standard, you must first fully realize the Way of that standard. Its Way is nothing other than that of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, extending to □’s □ [?]…

title: 成化十四年進士登科錄
text:
王夏法
祖宗於歷朝中者固已體行之矣今欲推而廣之非有甚
高難行之事也
陛下事天以誠恒若上帝之臨一有變異即弭之以實政
撫民以信常如赤子之保一有饑饉即賑之以實惠
是可謂之忠矣今欲民之不變詐也不過即此忠而
推之如發一令也信如四時行一政也堅如金石慎
簡大僚任以腹心而勿貳精擇諫臣寄以耳目而勿
疑賞必當功而不僭罰必當罪而不濫矯偽者必誅
告訐者不宥則民皆將化而為篤實夫焉有變詐多
===
訟者哉
陛下恭以持己而遊畋之事未嘗暫行儉以律身而服御
之物無所增飾是可謂之質矣今欲民之不奢靡也
不過即此質而推之勿以耳目之玩費民財勿以土
木之興竭民力裁減冗員不使蠹吾國也攘□游食
不使蠹吾民也禁奢侈必先近戚限田產必先貴家
則民皆將化而為儉約又焉有奢靡踰分者哉
陛下幸太學以勸天下之士祀先聖而加天子之禮綱目
成書昭百王之監戒勲戚就學振六館之文風是又
可□□矣今欲民之不粗鄙也亦惟即此文而推

punctuated:
王夏法祖宗於歷朝中者，固已體行之矣。今欲推而廣之，非有甚高難行之事也。

陛下事天以誠，恒若上帝之臨；一有變異，即弭之以實政。撫民以信，常如赤子之保；一有饑饉，即賑之以實惠。是可謂之忠矣。今欲民之不變詐也，不過即此忠而推之。如發一令也，信如四時；行一政也，堅如金石。慎簡大僚，任以腹心而勿貳；精擇諫臣，寄以耳目而勿疑。賞必當功而不僭，罰必當罪而不濫。矯偽者必誅，告訐者不宥，則民皆將化而為篤實，夫焉有變詐多訟者哉？

陛下恭以持己，而遊畋之事未嘗暫行；儉以律身，而服御之物無所增飾。是可謂之質矣。今欲民之不奢靡也，不過即此質而推之。勿以耳目之玩費民財，勿以土木之興竭民力。裁減冗員，不使蠹吾國也；攘□游食，不使蠹吾民也。禁奢侈必先近戚，限田產必先貴家，則民皆將化而為儉約，又焉有奢靡踰分者哉？

陛下幸太學以勸天下之士，祀先聖而加天子之禮。綱目成書，昭百王之監戒；勲戚就學，振六館之文風。是又可□□矣。今欲民之不粗鄙也，亦惟即此文而推
translation_en:
…[The opening words 王夏法 are unclear.] The imperial ancestors through successive reigns have indeed already embodied and practiced it [?]. To extend and broaden it now requires nothing so lofty as to be difficult to carry out.

Your Majesty serves Heaven with sincerity, always as though the Lord on High were present. Whenever an anomaly occurs, you counter it through substantive measures of government. You care for the people with good faith, always as though protecting an infant. Whenever famine occurs, you relieve them with tangible assistance. This may be called wholehearted sincerity. If you now wish the people to refrain from deceit, you need only extend this sincerity. In issuing an order, be as dependable as the four seasons; in implementing a measure, be as firm as metal and stone. Carefully select high officials, entrust them with the responsibilities of intimate confidants, and do not waver in your trust. Choose remonstrating officials with discernment, charge them to serve as your eyes and ears, and do not suspect them. Rewards must match merit without exceeding what is deserved; punishments must match offenses without indiscriminate severity. Those who practice deception must be punished, and those who maliciously denounce others must not be pardoned. Then the people will all be transformed into honest and steadfast persons. How could there still be deceitful people given to litigation?

Your Majesty conducts yourself with reverence and has never indulged even briefly in pleasure excursions or hunting. You discipline yourself through frugality, adding no embellishments to your clothing or articles of personal use. This may be called simplicity. If you now wish the people to refrain from extravagance, you need only extend this simplicity. Do not expend the people's wealth on amusements for the eyes and ears; do not exhaust their strength by undertaking construction works. Reduce superfluous officials, so that they do not drain our state; drive away [?] those who live idly at others' expense, so that they do not drain our people. Prohibitions on extravagance must begin with your close relatives, and limits on landed property must begin with noble households. Then the people will all be transformed into frugal and restrained persons. How could there still be those whose extravagance exceeds their station?

Your Majesty visits the Imperial University to encourage the scholars of the realm and sacrifices to the Former Sage with the full rites of the Son of Heaven. The completed Outline and Details (Gangmu) makes clear the instructive warnings furnished by the rulers of successive ages. Meritorious nobles and imperial relatives attend school, invigorating the literary culture of the six colleges. This, too, may be called [two characters illegible]. If you now wish the people to cease being coarse and uncultivated, you need only take this cultural refinement and extend it…

□□□加於大臣廉耻厲夫群臣選循良之守令
不以催科為能而以教養為最擇學行之師儒不徒
課以文詞而必迪以道德三物之教不徒行於庠序
之士而五禮之儀亦徧施於比閭之民則人皆將化
而為禮義亦何有乎粗鄙而鮮禮者哉誠如是則敝
無不革俗無不正而民悉囿于
皇極之中矣然究其推行之始則又在
陛下之一心耳昔堯舜禹之以中相授也必丁寧於人心
道心之告戒湯文武之以中相承也亦始於制心宅
心之功蓋人之心一而已一念之發生於形氣之私
===
則為人心原於性命之正則為道心形氣之私聲色
臭味之欲也性命之正仁義禮智之理也人心之發
而無以裁制之則物欲日滋而中道失雖欲言治皆
苟而已道心之發而無以汨喪之則理義日明而中
道得雖欲不治不可得也古今天下治亂之幾端不
出此臣願
陛下於退朝清燕之時察其心之所發其生於形氣之私
而為人心耶則用力克治不使之滋長其原於性命
之正而為道心耶則一意持守不使之變遷必使道
心常為一身之主而人心每聽命焉則動靜云為自

苟而已道心之發而無以涵養之則理義日□而中
道得雖欲不治不可得也古今天下治亂之端不
出此臣願
陛下於退朝清燕之時察其心之所發其生於形氣之私
而為人心耶則用力克治不使之滋長其原於性命
之正而為道心耶則一意持守不使之變遷必使道
心一身之主而人心每聽命焉則動靜云為自
punctuated:
□□□加於大臣，廉耻厲夫群臣。選循良之守令，不以催科為能，而以教養為最；擇學行之師儒，不徒課以文詞，而必迪以道德。三物之教，不徒行於庠序之士，而五禮之儀，亦徧施於比閭之民，則人皆將化而為禮義，亦何有乎粗鄙而鮮禮者哉？誠如是，則敝無不革，俗無不正，而民悉囿于皇極之中矣。然究其推行之始，則又在陛下之一心耳。
昔堯舜禹之以中相授也，必丁寧於人心道心之告戒；湯文武之以中相承也，亦始於制心宅心之功。蓋人之心一而已，一念之發，生於形氣之私，則為人心；原於性命之正，則為道心。形氣之私，聲色臭味之欲也；性命之正，仁義禮智之理也。人心之發而無以裁制之，則物欲日滋而中道失，雖欲言治，皆苟而已；道心之發而無以汨喪之，則理義日明而中道得，雖欲不治，不可得也。古今天下治亂之幾端，不出此。臣願陛下於退朝清燕之時，察其心之所發：其生於形氣之私而為人心耶，則用力克治，不使之滋長；其原於性命之正而為道心耶，則一意持守，不使之變遷。必使道心常為一身之主，而人心每聽命焉，則動靜云為自

…[Three illegible characters] applied to the high ministers [?], and integrity and a sense of shame used to exhort all officials. Select upright and benevolent prefects and magistrates, judging their ability not by their collection of taxes but giving highest merit to their instruction and nurture of the people. Choose teachers of learning and good conduct; do not merely assess them through literary composition, but require them to guide others through the Way and virtue. Let instruction in the three subjects—virtues, conduct, and arts—extend beyond the scholars in the schools, and let the forms of the five categories of rites likewise be practiced throughout the neighborhood communities. Then all people will be transformed and become observant of ritual propriety and righteousness. How could any remain coarse and deficient in propriety? If this is truly done, every abuse will be reformed, every custom rectified, and all the people brought within the supreme imperial standard. Yet, tracing this undertaking to its beginning, it rests solely in Your Majesty’s own heart.
When Yao, Shun, and Yu transmitted the Mean to one another, they invariably gave earnest admonitions concerning the human mind and the mind of the Way. When Tang, Wen, and Wu successively inherited the Mean, they too began with the work of regulating and settling the mind. A person has but one mind. When a thought arises from the private concerns of the bodily constitution, it constitutes the human mind; when it originates in the correctness of one’s nature and Heaven’s endowment, it constitutes the mind of the Way. The private concerns of the bodily constitution are desires for sounds, sights, smells, and tastes; the correctness of one’s nature and Heaven’s endowment consists in the principles of benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom. If the human mind arises and nothing restrains it, material desires increase daily and the Way of the Mean is lost. Even if one wishes to speak of good government, everything amounts merely to expediency. If the mind of the Way arises and nothing obscures or destroys it, principle and righteousness become clearer each day and the Way of the Mean is attained. Even if one wished to avoid good government, one could not. The incipient causes of order and disorder throughout the realm, past and present, lie entirely in this.
Your servant wishes that Your Majesty, in the quiet leisure following court, would examine what arises in your mind. Does it arise from the private concerns of the bodily constitution and thus constitute the human mind? Then exert yourself to overcome and regulate it, preventing its growth. Does it originate in the correctness of your nature and Heaven’s endowment and thus constitute the mind of the Way? Then preserve it single-mindedly, preventing it from changing. You must ensure that the mind of the Way always governs your whole person, and that the human mind always obeys its commands. Then, in activity and stillness, speech and action, you will naturally…

…[seven illegible characters] [?]; the Way is thereby established, and laws issue from it. In governing the realm, whatever Your Majesty wishes to accomplish will accord fully with your intentions. We shall then see you stand as a third alongside the Two Emperors and a fourth alongside the Three Kings, bringing glory to your ancestors’ magnificent achievements and transmitting an enduring imperial succession for ten thousand generations. All this proceeds from this same foundation.
The Song Confucian scholar Zhang Shi once said: “In answering at court, speaking frankly is of the utmost importance. When a scholar first appears before his ruler and father, this is his very first step. If he can deceive at this moment, there will be no occasion on which he will not deceive.” Your servant has often recited these words, regarding them as a memorable saying. Now that I have been granted this great opportunity to answer before the throne, how could I dare fail to speak frankly and thus deceive my ruler and father? I humbly beseech Your Sagely Majesty to give this your attention. It would be the greatest good fortune for the realm and for ten thousand generations. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

臣對：臣聞帝王之致治，必本乎中；帝王之用中，必因乎時。蓋中乃為治之本，而因時又用中之要也。為治不本乎中，則偏廢而治有所不舉；用中不因乎時，則膠固不通，又何以成其治哉？故善為治者，未有不本乎中；而善用中者，未有不因乎時。《書》曰：「允執厥中。」又曰：「動惟厥時。」正此謂也。君天下者，誠能因時用中，而盡時中之道，則治民而民無不從，教民而民無不化。變詐由是而忠厚，奢靡由是而儉朴，粗鄙由是而禮義，可以囿斯世於皇極之中，而天下風俗一歸于純正矣。尚何敝之有哉？大哉，時中乎！其為帝王出治之大本、為政之要道乎！二帝之所以帝天下而同守一道者，固時中之道也；三王之所以王天下而各有所尚者，亦此時中之道也。降及春秋、漢、唐、宋之治，所以不古若者，得非由其偏廢膠固，而不知所謂立中時中之道也歟？

translation_en:
Your servant, Zeng Zhui [?].
Your servant replies: I have heard that emperors and kings, in bringing about good government, must take the Mean as their foundation; and in applying the Mean, they must act according to the times. The Mean is the foundation of government, while adapting to the times is the essential condition for applying it. If government is not founded upon the Mean, partiality and neglect will leave some affairs unattended to. If the Mean is applied without regard to the times, rigid adherence will obstruct its operation: how, then, can good government be achieved? Thus, none who govern well fail to ground themselves in the Mean, and none who apply the Mean well fail to adapt to the times. The Book of Documents says, “Sincerely hold fast to the Mean,” and also, “Act only at the proper time.” This is precisely what these words mean. If the ruler of all under Heaven can truly apply the Mean according to the times and fully realize the Way of timeliness in the Mean, then when he governs the people, none will fail to obey; when he instructs them, none will fail to be transformed. Deceitfulness will thereby become loyalty and generosity, extravagance will become frugality and simplicity, and coarseness will give way to ritual propriety and righteousness. He can thus bring this age within the Mean of the sovereign’s supreme standard, and the customs of all under Heaven will return entirely to purity and correctness. What abuses could remain? Great indeed is timeliness in the Mean! Is it not the great foundation from which emperors and kings establish order, and the essential Way of government? The Way by which the Two Emperors ruled all under Heaven as emperors, both adhering to a single Way, was indeed this Way of timeliness in the Mean. The Way by which the Three Kings ruled all under Heaven as kings, each esteeming something different, was likewise this Way of timeliness in the Mean. Coming down to the Spring and Autumn period and the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, might their failure to equal antiquity in government not have resulted from their partiality, neglect, and rigid adherence, and their ignorance of what is called the Way of establishing the Mean and observing it according to the times?
I reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor is endowed with intelligence and sagacious understanding, and possesses the virtues of benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom. You are firm and vigorous, balanced and upright, accomplished in civil and military affairs, sagely and wondrous. Since ascending the throne, you have personally heard matters and rendered decisions, modeling your actions upon your imperial ancestors, directing the central mechanisms of government, and striving to bring about order and peace. You are truly what is called a ruler who appears but rarely in the ages. Yet you remain free of self-satisfaction and have summoned us, your servants, into …

translation_en:
…[?] Your inquiry extends to the means of securing good government and instruction. [?] That it reaches this point is a blessing for the altars of soil and grain and for the people. We, your servants, are ourselves among those subject to government and instruction. We never expected to be admitted together to the court and thereby fulfill our aspirations. How could we dare not lay bare what we hold within, to acknowledge and extol the gracious command of the sagely Son of Heaven? We have reverently read the imperial policy question, which states: “The sage kings of the Three Dynasties each esteemed something different in transforming and perfecting the world: the Xia esteemed loyalty, the Shang simplicity, and the Zhou refinement. Their dynasties endured for long periods; can the traces of their achievements be specifically described? Since the beginning of human life, those speaking of consummate government have invariably cited Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties. Now, if we speak only of the Three Dynasties without mentioning Tang and Yu, does this mean that Tang and Yu alone had nothing they particularly esteemed?”
Your servant considers that people are born with desires and fall into disorder without a ruler. Heaven therefore establishes rulers to lead them and teachers to instruct them. Those who act as rulers and teachers must strive reverently to follow Heaven’s mandate, so as to transform and perfect the world. Yet is there any other way to accomplish this? It consists simply in applying the mean according to the times. For the mean has no fixed form: it exists in accordance with the circumstances of each age. Thus, in governing the world, sage emperors and enlightened kings retained what ought to be retained and changed what ought to be changed. Between continuity and reform, they fashioned measures appropriate to the times. Hence, although they did not actually change the Way, they could not avoid what was called changing institutions. From Tang and Yu onward, the Xia, Shang, and Zhou arose in succession and enjoyed the longest dynastic reigns. That what they esteemed could not [?] differ was a consequence of what the times required. The Han scholar Dong Zhongshu said: “The Xia esteemed loyalty, the Shang simplicity, and the Zhou refinement.” Surely the kings of the Three Dynasties did not delight in being different for its own sake! During those dynasties, prevailing customs gradually developed and people’s hearts became increasingly mixed; the circumstances of the times exerted their influence. Thus their institutions tended daily toward greater elaboration. The Xia rulers succeeded Yu in governing, and in their unadulterated simplicity still retained a spirit of loyalty and sincerity. Consider how they put rewards before punishments and gave precedence to ranks [?]; [the text is unclear here] demanded perfection of a single person, did not expect too much of the common people, and in sacrifices used the dark …

求備焉祭則尚乎醴酒葬則先乎祭器其所以導民
者固異於夏之忠亦未及乎周之文也商政亡以衰武
王起而代之於是大有更張粲然文釆之盛觀其
賞罰用乎爵列祭祀尚乎旨酒謚號繁而道民以廣
孝盟詛作而約民以必信取於民則貢法助法之兼
行厚於親則明器祭器之兼用所以導民者視夏商

定名也乃後人因其不同而指名之耳三代而上唐
虞治化最為隆盛三代既各有所尚而唐虞獨無所
尚者蓋唐虞之際風氣未散人心未漓時乎無為也
是以堯之命舜惟曰執中是堯之道舜未嘗變也舜
之命禹亦曰執中是舜之道禹未嘗變也在上者惟
知有道德之隆在下者惟知享道化之盛渾渾噩噩

三代所尚如此，亦非固為是定尚而立是定名也，乃後人因其不同而指名之耳。三代而上，唐虞治化最為隆盛。三代既各有所尚，而唐虞獨無所尚者，蓋唐虞之際，風氣未散，人心未漓，時乎無為也。是以堯之命舜，惟曰執中，是堯之道舜未嘗變也；舜之命禹，亦曰執中，是舜之道禹未嘗變也。在上者惟知有道德之隆，在下者惟知享道化之盛，渾渾噩噩，無得而稱焉，又果何尚之可名乎？然則唐虞之無□□，聖聖相繼，同守此中而不異也；商周之有所□□，亂反正，因時救弊，亦斟酌損益以就此中也。
translation_en:
…[?] funerary objects. The means by which they guided the people all sprang from loyalty, without yet having [?]; what need, then, had they for Zhou’s refinement? When Xia’s government lost its order, Cheng Tang arose and replaced it. Although he made adjustments to government, an underlying simplicity remained. Consider how punishment preceded reward, service to spirits preceded ritual propriety, oaths were instituted because the people were not yet trustworthy, and complete performance was demanded of the people where they were not yet capable. In sacrifices, sweet wine was preferred; in burials, sacrificial vessels took precedence. The means by which they guided the people certainly differed from Xia’s loyalty, but had not yet reached Zhou’s refinement. When Shang’s government declined [?], King Wu arose and replaced it. Thereupon extensive changes were made, and brilliant cultural refinement became increasingly manifest. Consider how rewards and punishments were applied according to noble rank, and fine wine was preferred in sacrifices. Posthumous titles multiplied, guiding the people to extend their filial devotion; covenants and imprecations were instituted, binding the people to keep faith. In levying contributions from the people, both the tribute method and the labor-assistance method were employed; in showing generosity toward deceased kin, both funerary objects and sacrificial vessels were used. Thus the means by which they guided the people were more elaborate than those of Xia and Shang.

Such were the respective preferences of the Three Dynasties. They did not deliberately establish these fixed preferences and assign them fixed names; rather, later generations named them according to their differences. Before the Three Dynasties, government and moral transformation reached their greatest flourishing under Tang and Yu. Each of the Three Dynasties had its particular preference, whereas Tang and Yu alone had none, because in the age of Tang and Yu the prevailing moral spirit had not yet dispersed and people’s hearts had not yet become diluted. It was an age suited to governing through nonaction. Thus, when Yao charged Shun, he said only, “Hold fast to the mean.” This shows that Shun never changed Yao’s Way. When Shun charged Yu, he likewise said, “Hold fast to the mean.” This shows that Yu never changed Shun’s Way. Those above knew only the flourishing of the Way and virtue; those below knew only the enjoyment of abundant transformation through the Way. All was undifferentiated simplicity, beyond description. What particular preference could possibly be named? Thus, Tang and Yu’s lack of [?] meant that sage succeeded sage, together preserving this mean without deviation. Shang and Zhou’s having [?], restoring order from disorder, and remedying abuses according to the times likewise involved weighing what to diminish and what to augment in order to attain this mean.

異道哉
謂三王之道若循環終而復始春秋變周之
之質豈時然乎質法天文法地果然否乎漢損
周之文用夏之忠有所據乎唐宋二代歷年亦久有定
尚乎臣惟三王之法雖經久而可行三代之季亦有時
而或敝故司馬遷曰三王之道若循環終而復始夫
豈固為是相戾哉蓋夏人尚忠其失流於野救野之
失莫如質故殷人承之以質殷人尚質其失流於鬼
救鬼之失莫如文故周人承之以文周人尚文其失
流於薄救薄之失莫如忠是則三王之道承衰救敝
===
窮則反本亦時不得不然耳若夫殷人列爵惟公侯
伯之三等武王增以子男而為五等春秋之書合伯
子男而為一進夷狄皆稱子者是欲變周之文從殷
之質也且天道本下親親而質省故王者始起先本
天道以治天下而質家爵三等者豈非法天之有三
光乎地道敬上尊尊而文煩故後王起法地道以治
天下而文家爵五等者豈非法地之有五行乎何休
釋經若此而聖人之為政因時損益之意亦可見矣
炎漢之興適繼大亂之後救亂之敝莫若損周之文
用夏之忠苟不若三代之更制而襲因循之□

異道哉？
謂三王之道若循環，終而復始，春秋變周之之質，豈時然乎？質法天，文法地，果然否乎？漢損周之文，用夏之忠，有所據乎？唐宋二代歷年亦久，有定尚乎？
臣惟三王之法，雖經久而可行，三代之季，亦有時而或敝。故司馬遷曰：「三王之道若循環，終而復始。」夫豈固為是相戾哉？蓋夏人尚忠，其失流於野，救野之失，莫如質，故殷人承之以質；殷人尚質，其失流於鬼，救鬼之失，莫如文，故周人承之以文；周人尚文，其失流於薄，救薄之失，莫如忠。是則三王之道，承衰救敝，窮則反本，亦時不得不然耳。若夫殷人列爵，惟公侯伯之三等，武王增以子男而為五等；春秋之書，合伯子男而為一，進夷狄皆稱子者，是欲變周之文，從殷之質也。且天道本下，親親而質省，故王者始起，先本天道以治天下，而質家爵三等者，豈非法天之有三光乎？地道敬上，尊尊而文煩，故後王起，法地道以治天下，而文家爵五等者，豈非法地之有五行乎？何休釋經若此，而聖人之為政，因時損益之意，亦可見矣。炎漢之興，適繼大亂之後，救亂之敝，莫若損周之文，用夏之忠。苟不若三代之更制，而襲因循之□
translation_en:
…could these be different Ways?
It is said that the Way of the Three Kings resembles a cycle, beginning again when it reaches its end, and that the Spring and Autumn Annals changed Zhou’s [refinement to] simplicity [?]. Was this brought about by the times? Simplicity models itself on Heaven, and refinement on Earth: is this indeed so? Was there a basis for the Han’s reducing Zhou’s refinement and employing Xia’s wholehearted sincerity? The Tang and Song dynasties likewise lasted many years: did each have a settled preference?
Your servant considers that, although the institutions of the Three Kings remained practicable over long periods, abuses sometimes arose toward the end of each of the Three Dynasties. Thus Sima Qian said: “The Way of the Three Kings resembles a cycle, beginning again when it reaches its end.” Surely they did not deliberately set themselves at odds with one another! The people of Xia esteemed wholehearted sincerity, but its failings degenerated into uncouthness. Nothing remedies uncouthness better than simplicity, so the people of Yin succeeded them with simplicity. The people of Yin esteemed simplicity, but its failings degenerated into preoccupation with spirits. Nothing remedies this failing better than refinement, so the people of Zhou succeeded them with refinement. The people of Zhou esteemed refinement, but its failings degenerated into superficiality. Nothing remedies superficiality better than wholehearted sincerity. Thus the Way of the Three Kings was to remedy abuses inherited from a declining age and, when an approach was exhausted, return to the root. The times themselves made this unavoidable.
As for the ranks of nobility established by the people of Yin, there were only three: duke, marquis, and earl. King Wu added viscount and baron, making five ranks. The Spring and Autumn Annals combined earls, viscounts, and barons into a single category, and, when advancing the status of the Yi and Di peoples, called all their rulers viscounts. This expressed the wish to change Zhou’s refinement and follow Yin’s simplicity. Moreover, the Way of Heaven takes what is below as its foundation, cherishes kin, and is simple and sparing. Thus, when true kings first arose, they began by basing their government of the world on the Way of Heaven. Was not the establishment of three noble ranks by dynasties favoring simplicity modeled on Heaven’s Three Luminaries? The Way of Earth reveres what is above, honors the exalted, and is elaborate in its forms. Thus later kings arose and modeled their government of the world on the Way of Earth. Was not the establishment of five noble ranks by dynasties favoring refinement modeled on Earth’s Five Phases? He Xiu interpreted the classic in this way, and here too one can discern the sages’ intention in governing: to subtract or add according to the times.
The rise of the Han, associated with the virtue of Fire, came immediately after great disorder. To remedy the abuses of disorder, nothing was better than reducing Zhou’s refinement and employing Xia’s wholehearted sincerity. If, instead of changing institutions as the Three Dynasties had done, it had perpetuated the [illegible] of merely following established practice…

制策又曰我
太祖高皇帝肇造洪業
列聖相承益隆治教百餘年來海內漸涵仁義之〔澤厚矣〕
其所尚可名乎若名曰忠民情猶變詐而多訟非忠也
若名曰質民用猶奢靡而踰分非質也若名曰文民俗
猶粗鄙而鮮禮非文也名既不可然則今之世其如唐

punctuated:
□□繼秦矣。董仲舒告武帝若此，以漢之為政，因時救敝之術所當然也。自漢而後，稱善治者必曰唐、宋。李唐一代，享國垂三百年，不為不久也。以言所尚，太宗大召學士，天下崇文，若文矣。然用工靡麗，無補踐履，其視周之文，奚啻螢爝之比日月也！趙宋一代，享國踰三百年，不為不永也。以言所尚，太祖以仁厚得國，恭儉化民，若質矣。然制度因五代之陋，禮樂無三代之意，其視商之質，奚啻碔砆之與美玉也！夫漢、唐、宋所尚不能媲美三代者，蓋其為治不過牽補過時，架漏度日，不能大有所更張，以合乎時中之道故也。

制策又曰：「我太祖高皇帝肇造洪業，列聖相承，益隆治教，百餘年來，海內漸涵仁義之日厚矣。其所尚可名乎？若名曰忠，民情猶變詐而多訟，非忠也；若名曰質，民用猶奢靡而踰分，非質也；若名曰文，民俗猶粗鄙而鮮禮，非文也。名既不可，然則今之世，其如唐虞之無所尚乎？朕欲移風易俗，去其所謂忠敬文之敝，悉囿斯人于皇極之中，行之自何始？」臣惟我
translation_en:
…[two illegible characters] succeeded Qin [?]. Dong Zhongshu spoke thus to Emperor Wu because, in governing the Han, adapting to the times and remedying abuses was necessarily the proper course. After the Han, those who speak of good government invariably name the Tang and Song. The Li house’s Tang dynasty held the realm for nearly three hundred years: its duration was certainly not short. As for what it esteemed, Taizong summoned scholars in great numbers, and all under Heaven honored cultural refinement; this would seem to exemplify refinement. Yet effort was spent on ornate embellishment, without contributing to actual practice. Compared with Zhou refinement, how could it be anything more than the light of fireflies and torches beside the sun and moon! The Zhao house’s Song dynasty held the realm for over three hundred years: its duration was certainly long. As for what it esteemed, Taizu won the realm through benevolence and generosity, and transformed the people through respectfulness and frugality; this would seem to exemplify simplicity. Yet its institutions perpetuated the shortcomings of the Five Dynasties, and its rites and music lacked the spirit of the Three Dynasties. Compared with Shang simplicity, how could it be anything more than a jade-like stone beside fine jade! The qualities esteemed by the Han, Tang, and Song could not match those of the Three Dynasties because their governments merely patched things together to get through the times and propped up leaking structures to get through the days. They could not undertake substantial reforms to accord with the Way of attaining the mean appropriate to the time.

The imperial policy question further says: “Our Emperor Taizu Gao founded the great enterprise. The succession of sage emperors increasingly exalted government and moral instruction, and for more than a hundred years all within the seas have been ever more deeply steeped in benevolence and righteousness. Can the quality our dynasty esteems be named? If it is called wholehearted sincerity, the people’s dispositions are still deceitful and prone to litigation: this is not sincerity. If it is called simplicity, the people’s expenditure is still extravagant and exceeds the bounds of their stations: this is not simplicity. If it is called refinement, popular customs are still coarse and lacking in ritual propriety: this is not refinement. Since none of these names applies, is the present age then like the ages of Tang and Yu, which esteemed no single quality? Yet Your Majesty’s sagely heart still worries that the people are deceitful rather than loyal, extravagant rather than plain, and coarse rather than refined, and wishes to bring about their transformation. Here I perceive Your Majesty’s disposition: the more fully accomplished you are, the more you regard yourself as insufficient; the nearer you come to perfection, the more you seek it.
Your servant humbly believes that transforming the people’s deceitfulness begins with Your Majesty leading them through loyalty and trustworthiness. For, as the saying goes, “Through thoroughness one attains a good end” [?]; the Xia king’s establishment of a line of succession was indeed founded upon loyalty and trustworthiness. The deceitfulness of those below arises simply because those above have failed to establish loyalty and trustworthiness. If every policy put into effect is as firm as metal and stone, and every command proclaimed as dependable as the four seasons; if rewards invariably match merit, without indiscriminate grants, and punishments invariably match offenses, without excessive penalties; if preferences and aversions, taking and giving, are free from error, and seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting are free from impropriety; and if malicious informers are punished and deceivers put to death—then none among the people will fail to be loyal. Deceitful customs can be transformed and brought back to sincerity. How could their attendant evils remain?
Transforming the people’s extravagance begins with Your Majesty setting them right through an example of frugality. For, as the saying goes, “Attend carefully to your virtue of frugality”; the Shang house’s succession to rule was indeed founded upon frugality. The extravagance of those below arises simply because those above do not practice this virtue. If the example of Your Majesty’s own conduct takes the lead in the palace, and the transforming influence of wearing washed garments extends throughout the inner court; if unwarranted expenditure is reduced and nonessential building projects are discontinued; if those who trim their shoes with embroidered brocade are punished and covering walls with patterned silk is prohibited—then none among the people will fail to be plain. Extravagant customs can be transformed and brought back to frugality. How could their attendant evils remain? As for transforming the people’s coarseness, its implementation …

今日所以因時救敝化民成俗所謂時中之道者端不
出此
===

以獻朕將親覽焉臣草茅微士樗櫟庸材今何幸以一

translation_en:
…Set forth the five fundamental human relationships, harmonize the people's standards of conduct, and guide them with □ [?]. These words describe how Kings Wen and Wu taught the people. The coarseness of those below arises because those above sometimes relax their teaching of established norms. If the strengthening of the five relationships proceeds entirely from the expression of sincere intent, and the practice of the five rites entirely from the mutual trust inspired by genuine virtue; if proper institutions are established to guard against deviant tendencies, and orderly forms of conduct guide those who fall short; if teaching in the schools is clearly expounded and instruction in the local communities rigorously enforced, and the people of the neighborhood groupings—bi, lü, zu, and dang—are registered according to their conduct in filial devotion, brotherly affection, harmony among relatives, and concord with relatives by marriage: then coarse customs will begin to change, and all the people will become refined. What evil of uncultivated conduct could then remain? Loyalty and trustworthiness, frugality, and established norms constitute the supreme virtue and essential Way of the former kings. The means today of remedying abuses as circumstances require and transforming the people and their customs—the so-called Way of attaining the Mean appropriate to the time—lie wholly within these.
At the end of the imperial policy question, Your Majesty further states: “You students have long studied the Classics and awaited questioning. Now that you have all come to court, set forth your views in detail and submit them. I shall examine them personally.” Your servant is an insignificant scholar from the countryside, a man of commonplace ability, as useless as the ailanthus or the scrub oak. How fortunate I am now that even a single insight from my foolish understanding may trouble Your Majesty's lofty gaze! Reflecting that my daily studies have been devoted to the Classics, how could I presume to search elsewhere and introduce far-fetched citations? I respectfully draw two propositions from the Classics as my offering at the close of this essay.
The first is to preserve sincerity as the great foundation of this Mean. For although the Mean is the great foundation from which good government proceeds, sincerity is in turn the great foundation of this Mean. Why is this so? To be genuine and without falsity is called sincerity; to be pure and unmixed is called sincerity. Sincerity accords with Heaven; insincerity belongs to the merely human. Sincerity accords with principle; insincerity with desire. Sincerity brings clarity and understanding; insincerity brings obstruction. When sincerity is preserved within, the substance of this Mean is established; when sincerity manifests itself outwardly, the operation of this Mean is realized. Yao's sincere holding fast, Shun's fullness of sincerity, Yu's earnest acceptance of difficulty, Tang's sincere virtue bringing harmony to those below, and Wen and Wu's attainment of the utmost …

二帝三王之中，未有不本於誠者。苟中而不，或涉於渺茫，或淪於空虛，而非帝王之所謂□□。願皇上本誠以體此中，必純乎天，不間以人；純乎理，不雜以欲；純乎明通，不混以否塞。昕臨大廷，百辟星布，此時固誠矣，不可以深宮大內少有所間焉。日御講帷，學士雲集，此時固誠矣，不可以燕居獨處少有所息焉。存誠之功，不以頃刻而有間，則此心之中皆實物矣。形而為因時之治，尚何不足變民俗而廣皇極之化哉？

二曰：用賢以為執中之助。盖治固以中道而後成，而中又必資賢以為輔。何則？三德六德之謂賢，即宅即俊之謂賢。賢人多，能升其國於明昌；小人衆，能降其國於晻昧。賢者能輔君而成化，小人則妨賢而病國。賢人用于左右，則此中之德成于上；賢人列于庶位，則此中之澤溥于下。帝堯之明明揚側陋，虞舜之用賢勿貳，夏商之籲俊尊帝，成湯之敷求哲人，文武之庶官用上，二帝三王之中，未有不資賢以為輔者。苟中而不資於賢焉，則或鑿以自私，或狃□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□不□□□□□□體中矣。臣願
translation_en:
…The equilibrium of the Two Emperors and Three Kings was invariably rooted in sincerity. If one pursues equilibrium without [sincerity?], one may stray into nebulousness or sink into emptiness; this is not what the emperors and kings called [illegible]. I wish that Your Majesty would take sincerity as the foundation for embodying this equilibrium: remain wholly aligned with Heaven, without human interference; wholly aligned with principle, without the admixture of desire; and wholly lucid and perceptive, without the confusion of obstruction. At dawn, when you preside over the great court and the officials stand arrayed like stars, you are certainly sincere; yet you must not allow the slightest interruption of that sincerity within the secluded palace and inner apartments. Each day, when you attend the imperial lectures and the scholars gather like clouds, you are certainly sincere; yet you must not allow the slightest cessation of it when resting privately or dwelling alone. If the effort to preserve sincerity suffers no interruption, even for an instant, then the equilibrium of this mind will be entirely substantial. When expressed in government responsive to the times, how could it fail to transform popular customs and extend the transforming influence of the August Ultimate?

Second: employ worthy men to assist in holding fast to the mean. Good government can indeed be achieved only through the Way of the Mean, and maintaining the mean necessarily requires the assistance of worthy men. Why is this so? Those who possess the Three Virtues and Six Virtues are called worthy; those described as taking their places and approaching the eminent are called worthy [?]. When worthy men are numerous, they can raise their state to enlightened prosperity; when petty men abound, they can bring their state down into darkness. Worthy men assist their ruler in accomplishing moral transformation; petty men obstruct the worthy and harm the state. When worthy men serve at the ruler’s side, the virtue of this equilibrium is perfected above; when worthy men occupy the various offices, its benefits spread widely below. Emperor Yao brought the illustrious to light and promoted men from obscure stations; Shun of Yu employed the worthy without wavering; Xia and Shang summoned eminent men to honor the Lord on High; Cheng Tang sought wise men far and wide; and Wen and Wu employed superior men in the various offices [?]. The equilibrium of the Two Emperors and Three Kings invariably relied on worthy men for assistance. If one pursues equilibrium without drawing upon worthy men, one may distort it through selfishness or become habituated to [illegible passage] … embody equilibrium [?]. Your servant wishes …

translation_en:
…[illegible] assist this mind at all times [?]; allow no interruption, and do not employ the crafty [illegible; the intervening wording is uncertain]. Whenever a thought first arises, be sure to discuss its merits with your assisting ministers; whenever a policy [illegible], be sure to deliberate with upright [illegible]. Forget not a single utterance or word, and be thorough in understanding and clear discernment. Some words that accord with your wishes should go unheeded; words that grate upon your ears should be those you delight to hear. If your determination to employ the worthy never slackens even for a moment, the application of this mean will naturally involve neither excess nor deficiency. When put into practice as government suited to the times, how could it fail to transform popular customs and extend the transforming influence of the imperial standard?

If this is done, the Way by which the ancient emperors and kings maintained the mean according to the circumstances will be fully realized in Your Majesty’s sagely mind, and their government according to that mean will appear again today. Thus you may become a third alongside the Two Emperors and a fourth alongside the Three Kings, bring glory to your ancestors, and bequeath abundance to posterity [the closing wording is garbled: 全意馬, ?]. Your servant has heard the saying of the ancients: “It is not knowing that is difficult; it is putting knowledge into practice that is difficult.” I humbly pray that Your Majesty will give these words some consideration and accept them, going beyond merely knowing them. Then all under Heaven will be most fortunate, and the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain most fortunate. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.
